Module 9

Toolsmith: the same tools on both systems

This is the capstone of the course. Instead of reading one more part of the two systems, you build small, useful command-line tools on both of them, the way their own utilities are built: in assembly, in C, and in the shell's script language (.BAT files on MS-DOS 4.00, sh scripts on FreeBSD 15.1). Six tools, each written for both systems, exercise every interface a tool depends on: how the arguments arrive, what the standard handles are and who redirects them, how an exit code travels back to the shell, how text files differ from binary files, how much memory a program gets, and how each system turns source text into something it can run.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.030 source listings2 study cases6 exercisesabout 135 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Every MS-DOS program in this module was built with the 1988 toolchain (tools/dos_tools.py, or NASM for .COM files) and run on the real MS-DOS 4.00 (tools/dos_run.py); every FreeBSD program was built and run in the course VM. All outputs are captured, not typed. Where MS-DOS 4.00 did something its own documentation does not promise, the source code explains why, and the text says so.

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • name, for each system, the exact mechanism that delivers arguments, the environment, the standard handles and the exit code to a program, and point to the source code that implements it;
  • write the same tool in assembly, in C and as a script on both systems, and choose the language that fits;
  • parse a DOS command tail and walk a FreeBSD argc/argv/envp stack without any library;
  • explain text and binary mode on MS-DOS (CR LF, Ctrl-Z, the C runtime's translation) and why FreeBSD has no such distinction;
  • follow an exit code from INT 21h function 4Ch to IF ERRORLEVEL, and from exit(3) through wait(2) to $?, including what happens to values above 255 and to programs killed by Ctrl-C or a signal;
  • write batch files and sh scripts that check every step, report what they did and return a meaningful exit code;
  • test a tool by redirecting its input from files and comparing its output with a reference, on a system where you cannot type at the keyboard;
  • discover and document a system's limitations from its source instead of from folklore.

Prerequisites. Module 3 (COMMAND.COM and sh: parsing, redirection, pipes, batch files, the environment), Module 4 (8086 and amd64 assembly), Module 5 (the toolchains, memory models, .COM, MZ and ELF, start-up code), Module 6 (the console and termios) and Module 8 (the DOS memory arena). You need the MS-DOS tools from Module 0 and the FreeBSD VM with nasm.

9.1 What a tool needs from the operating system#

A command-line tool has a small contract with the system that starts it. It receives some text that the user typed (its arguments) and a set of named strings (its environment). It finds three streams already open: input, output and errors. It may open files by name, it uses some memory, and when it finishes it hands back one small number. Neither kernel knows anything about options, wildcards or quoting; those are conventions of the shell and of the C library. Table 9.1 lists the mechanism behind each part of the contract.

Table 9.1 – The contract between a tool and the system

Need MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Arguments One string in the 128 bytes at PSP offset 80h: a length byte, then at most 127 bytes of text ending in a CR. EXEC copies 128 bytes from the caller (Listing 9.1) An array of separate NUL-terminated strings; argc and argv on the new stack (Listing 9.2); arguments and environment together up to ARG_MAX, 512 KB (syslimits.h line 44)
Splitting and wildcards The program: C start-up code splits the tail into argv (Module 5); wildcards only if the program asks The shell, before execve (Module 3); the program receives finished words
Program name After the environment strings, as a full path (Module 3, section 3.7) argv[0], whatever the caller chose; the kernel also passes the path as AT_EXECPATH in the auxiliary vector (imgact_elf.c line 1473)
Environment A segment of NAME=value strings; its address is the word at PSP offset 2Ch (PDB.INC line 27) envp, right after the NULL that ends argv (kern_exec.c lines 1810-1824)
Standard streams Handles 0-4 (input, output, error, AUX, PRN) in the 20-entry Job File Table at PSP offset 18h (PDB.INC lines 8 and 22) Descriptors 0, 1 and 2, inherited through fork and execve (Module 3)
First instruction .COM: CS = DS = ES = SS = PSP, IP = 100h, SP near the top of the segment (Listing 9.14) rip = ELF entry point, rdi = address of argc (Listing 9.3)
Exit code INT 21h function 4Ch with the code in AL; DOS keeps AL plus an exit type in AH (Listing 9.9); the parent asks with function 4Dh _exit(rval); the kernel keeps rval (kern_exit.c line 305) and hands 8 bits of it to wait4 (Listing 9.12)
Memory A .COM program receives the largest free block; an .EXE what its header asks for (Modules 5 and 8) A private virtual address space, bounded by resource limits (section 9.5)

On MS-DOS the arguments are a single line of text. COMMAND.COM removes the redirections from the line (Module 3, section 3.4), builds a command tail and calls EXEC, which copies it into the new program's PSP together with two FCBs parsed from the first two words, a convention left over from CP/M:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.1 – EXEC copies the command tail into the new PSP at 80h (EXEC.ASM lines 719-727)Source ↗
        POP     SI                      ; get block (last time)
        POP     DS
        LDS     SI,[SI.exec0_com_line]  ; command line
;
; DS points to user space 80 command line
;
        OR      CL,80h
        MOV     DI,CX
        REP     MOVSB                   ; Wham!

CX is zero after the previous FCB copy, so OR CL,80h makes it 128: the count and the destination offset are the same number. Whatever follows the command name, up to the CR, is now at PSP:81h, with its length at PSP:80h. Splitting it into words is the program's business. A program written in assembly does it by hand (Lab 9.1); a C program gets argc and argv from the start-up code, which splits the tail at blanks and handles double quotes (Module 5, section 5.5). Even the program's own name is not in the tail: EXEC writes it after the environment strings (Module 3, section 3.7).

On FreeBSD the shell has already split the line into words, expanded the wildcards and removed the quotes. execve copies the finished strings to the top of the new stack and builds the vectors below them:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.2 – exec_copyout_strings builds argv on the new process's stack (kern_exec.c lines 1795-1808)Source ↗
        /*
         * Fill in argument portion of vector table.
         */
        for (; argc > 0; --argc) {
                if (suword(vectp++, ustringp) != 0)
                        return (EFAULT);
                while (*stringp++ != 0)
                        ustringp++;
                ustringp++;
        }

        /* a null vector table pointer separates the argp's from the envp's */
        if (suword(vectp++, 0) != 0)
                return (EFAULT);

The environment pointers follow the same way, then the auxiliary vector. Finally the ELF image activator stores argc in the word below argv (imgact_elf.c lines 1536-1546), and the machine-dependent code sets the first registers:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.3 – The first registers of a new amd64 process (exec_machdep.c lines 433-436)Source ↗
        regs->tf_rip = imgp->entry_addr;
        regs->tf_rsp = ((stack - 8) & ~0xFul) + 8;
        regs->tf_rdi = stack;           /* argv */
        regs->tf_rflags = PSL_USER | saved_rflags;

rdi points at argc, with argv[0] at rdi+8. rsp is the same address rounded so that the stack is aligned the way the amd64 calling convention expects at a function entry, which means it can be 8 bytes below argc. The C start-up code in crt1.o uses rdi (Module 5, section 5.5), and so must an assembly program that has no start-up code (Lab 9.1). Figure 9.1 puts the two paths side by side.

The three standard streams are set up the same way on both systems: the shell arranges them before the program starts, and the program inherits them. COMMAND.COM edits its own Job File Table, so that handle 0 or 1 refers to the file named after < or >, calls EXEC (the child receives a copy of the table) and puts the table back afterwards (Module 3, section 3.4). sh forks; the child opens the file, moves it to descriptor 0 or 1 with dup2, and calls execve. Either way the tool just reads handle 0 and writes handle 1, and does not know where they lead unless it asks: INT 21h function 4400h (IOCTL "get device information") on MS-DOS, isatty(3) on FreeBSD. ASK (Lab 9.6) needs to ask. Two differences matter for tools. COMMAND.COM can redirect only handles 0 and 1, so an error message written to handle 2 always reaches the screen; sh can redirect any descriptor (2>). And a DOS "pipe" is two temporary files and two programs run one after the other (Module 3, section 3.5), so a tool in the middle of a DOS pipeline reads a file that has already been completely written.

9.2 Three ways to build a tool on each system#

Each system offers three ways to turn source text into a tool: assembly without any library, C with its library, and a script that the shell interprets. Figure 9.3 shows the six pipelines; Table 9.2 summarises what each produces.

Table 9.2 – What each pipeline produces

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Assembly, no library nasm -f bin writes a .COM file: a memory image loaded at offset 100h, no header, no linker. Or MASM, LINK and EXE2BIN (Module 5) nasm -f elf64 writes an object file; ld makes a static ELF executable that contains only your code and talks to the kernel with syscall
C CL /AS compiles to an .OBJ and LINK adds SLIBCE.LIB, giving an MZ .EXE with relocations and the C start-up code cc compiles and links against crt1.o and libc.so.7; the run-time linker finishes the job at start-up (Module 5)
Script A .BAT file, read and interpreted by COMMAND.COM one line at a time (Module 3, section 3.6) A text file with execute permission whose first line is #!/bin/sh; the kernel starts /bin/sh with the script's path
How the shell finds it Current directory, then each PATH directory; in each directory .COM before .EXE before .BAT (Listing 9.4) Each PATH directory in order; the current directory only if it is in PATH; the kernel decides by content, not by name

On MS-DOS the extension decides how a file is run, and the search prefers some extensions to others:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.4 – COMMAND.COM's search order (PATH2.ASM lines 84-96)Source ↗
;----------------------------------------------------------------------------
;   SEARCH, when given a pathname, attempts to find a file with
; one of the following extensions:  .com, .exe, .bat (highest to
; lowest priority).  Where conflicts arise, the extension with
; the highest priority is favored.
; ENTRY:
;   DX          --      pointer to null-terminated pathname
;   fbuf        --      dma buffer for findfirst/next
; EXIT:
;   AX          --      8)  file found with .com extension
;                       4)  file found with .exe extension
;                       2)  file found with .bat extension
;                       0)  no such file to be found

This matters as soon as two versions of a tool live in one directory. If ARGS.COM (assembly) and ARGS.EXE © are both there, ARGS runs the .COM; you must type ARGS.EXE for the other one, which the same routine honours (an explicit extension sets ext_entered). The lab disk also holds MS-DOS's own BACKUP.COM, so a batch file called BACKUP.BAT in the same directory can only be started as BACKUP.BAT (Lab 9.7). FreeBSD has the same trap in another form: a script called test in your directory loses to the shell's test builtin.

On FreeBSD the kernel looks at the first bytes of the file. An ELF header goes to the ELF image activator; the two characters #! go to the shell image activator, which rewrites the argument list:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.5 – How the kernel runs a script (imgact_shell.c lines 64-82)Source ↗
 * If the given file is a shell-script, then the first line will start
 * with the two characters `#!' (aka SHELLMAGIC), followed by the name
 * of the shell-interpreter to run, followed by zero or more tokens.
 *
 * The interpreter is then started up such that it will see:
 *    arg[0] -> The name of interpreter as specified after `#!' in the
 *              first line of the script.  The interpreter name must
 *              not be longer than MAXSHELLCMDLEN bytes.
 *    arg[1] -> *If* there are any additional tokens on the first line,
 *              then we add a new arg[1], which is a copy of the rest of
 *              that line.  The copy starts at the first token after the
 *              interpreter name.  We leave it to the interpreter to
 *              parse the tokens in that value.
 *    arg[x] -> the full pathname of the script.  This will either be
 *              arg[2] or arg[1], depending on whether or not tokens
 *              were found after the interpreter name.
 *  arg[x+1] -> all the arguments that were specified on the original
 *              command line.
 *

A script is therefore a program like any other: it can be started by execve, appears in ps under its interpreter's name, and returns an exit status through wait. A .BAT file is none of these. Only COMMAND.COM can run it, it is not a process, and it has no exit code of its own (section 9.4 and Lab 9.7).

The three pipelines also differ in size, start-up cost and what you can reach. The assembly ARGS.COM of Lab 9.1 is 251 bytes, all of them code and strings; the C ARGS.EXE is 7,287 bytes because it carries the start-up code and printf. The FreeBSD assembly version is a static ELF file of 2,176 bytes of which 264 are code: the rest is headers and symbols, and strip brings it down to 960. The C version is smaller than on MS-DOS (9,984 bytes) only because printf stays in the shared libc.so (Table 9.5 in section 9.6 has all the measured sizes). C buys portability: the same WC.C compiles on both systems with one #ifdef (Lab 9.3). Scripts buy the existing tools: BACKUP.BAT copies files with XCOPY and compares them with FC instead of reimplementing either.

9.3 Text and binary#

The MS-DOS kernel, like FreeBSD's, stores and returns bytes: INT 21h function 3Fh reads exactly what is in the file. Text is a convention on top. MS-DOS inherited two conventions from CP/M: lines end with CR LF (0Dh 0Ah), and Ctrl-Z (1Ah) marks the end of a text file, because CP/M recorded file sizes only in 128-byte records and padded the last record with Ctrl-Z. FAT records sizes to the byte, so the Ctrl-Z is no longer needed, but much DOS software still writes it and still stops reading when it sees one. The console device in cooked mode reports end of file on Ctrl-Z (Module 6, section 6.5), and so does TYPE:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.6 – TYPE stops at the first Ctrl-Z (TCMD1B.ASM lines 417-440)Source ↗
        mov     ah,read
        int     int_command
        jc      typerr                          ;AN022; Exit if error
        mov     cx,ax
        jcxz    typelp_ret                      ;AC000; exit if nothing read
        push    ds
        pop     es                              ; Check to see if a ^Z was read.
assume es:nothing
        xor     di,di
        push    ax
        mov     al,1ah
        repnz   scasb
        pop     ax
        xchg    ax,cx
        cmp     ax,0
        jnz     foundz                          ; Yes, handle it
        cmp     byte ptr [di-1],1ah             ; No, double check
        jnz     typecont2                       ; No ^Z, continue

foundz:
        sub     cx,ax                           ; Otherwise change cx so that only those
        dec     cx                              ;  bytes up to but NOT including the ^Z
        push    cs                              ;  will be typed.
        pop     es

COPY has both behaviours. With /A ("ASCII") it reads a source only up to the first Ctrl-Z (COPY.ASM lines 739-752) and appends one Ctrl-Z to an ASCII destination (COPY.ASM line 801); with /B, the default when one file is copied to another, it copies bytes. Concatenation (COPY A+B C) defaults to ASCII. CTRLZ.TXT in labs/09-toolsmith/dos has two lines, a Ctrl-Z and a third line:

Output 9.1 – TYPE, COPY /A and COPY on a file with an embedded Ctrl-Z (MS-DOS 4.00)
---- TYPE CTRLZ.TXT
line one
line two
---- COPY /A CTRLZ.TXT ZA.TXT
        1 File(s) copied
---- COPY CTRLZ.TXT ZB.TXT
        1 File(s) copied
---- DIR *Z*.TXT

 Volume in drive A is DOS400LAB
 Volume Serial Number is 1988-0400
 Directory of  A:\

CTRLZ    TXT        39 04-25-24  12:00p
ZA       TXT        21 04-25-24  12:00p
ZB       TXT        39 04-25-24  12:00p
        3 File(s)     273920 bytes free
---- FC /B CTRLZ.TXT ZA.TXT
fc: CTRLZ.TXT longer than ZA.TXT

The ASCII copy has 20 bytes of text plus the Ctrl-Z that COPY added; the third line is gone. A tool that treats every file as text would lose data in the same way, and that is exactly what the Microsoft C runtime does by default. Every stream and every opened file is in text mode unless the program says otherwise:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.7 – Text mode in Microsoft C 5.10 (FCNTL.H lines 22-27)Source ↗
/* O_TEXT files have <cr><lf> sequences translated to <lf> on read()'s,
** and <lf> sequences translated to <cr><lf> on write()'s
*/

#define O_TEXT      0x4000  /* file mode is text (translated) */
#define O_BINARY    0x8000  /* file mode is binary (untranslated) */

The header does not mention Ctrl-Z, and the runtime's source is not part of the MS-DOS tree, so Lab 9.4 measures it: in text mode a read stops at the first Ctrl-Z, as TYPE does. A program chooses binary mode in one of four ways: "rb" or "wb" in fopen; O_BINARY in open; setmode(fileno(stdin), O_BINARY) for a stream that is already open (IO.H line 38); or the global default _fmode (STDLIB.H line 87), which linking with BINMODE.OBJ sets to binary. A hex dump must see every byte, so HD (Lab 9.4) uses "rb" for files and setmode for standard input. WC is a text tool, but it must also count bytes the way DIR does, so it reads in binary mode too and counts LF characters as lines. Figure 9.4 shows the translation.

FreeBSD has one line ending, LF, and no end-of-file character; fopen accepts "b" because ISO C requires it, and ignores it:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.8 – FreeBSD's fopen ignores the binary flag (flags.c lines 77-82)Source ↗
        do {
                known = 1;
                switch (*mode++) {
                case 'b':
                        /* 'b' (binary) is ignored */
                        break;

The difference shows up when files cross between the systems. A DOS text file on FreeBSD has a CR before every LF: wc -l still counts the lines correctly, but wc -c counts one byte more per line, a shell script with CR LF endings fails with confusing errors (sh sees fi\r, not fi), and a stray Ctrl-Z at the end is just one more byte. Lab 9.3 counts the same test file on both systems.

9.4 Exit codes end to end#

An exit code is the one number a tool can return to whoever started it. On MS-DOS a program ends with INT 21h function 4Ch and the code in AL. $EXIT notes whether the program is ending normally or because of Ctrl-C (PROC.ASM lines 129-144), and the common termination code stores the type next to the code:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.9 – DOS keeps the exit code in AL and the exit type in AH (PROC.ASM lines 164-170)Source ↗
; from exit_type.  Also, the PDB at user_CS needs to be correct as the one
; that is terminating.
;
        entry   abort_inner

        MOV     AH,[exit_type]
        MOV     [exit_code],AX

The types are 0 for a normal end, 1 for Ctrl-C, 2 for a critical error and 3 for terminate-and-stay-resident (EXE.INC lines 42-46). When EXEC returns, COMMAND.COM asks for the code with function 4Dh, which returns the word and clears it (PROC.ASM lines 62-66), and saves it in RETCODE:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.10 – COMMAND.COM saves the exit code of an external command (COMMAND1.ASM lines 455-468)Source ↗
EXT_EXEC:
        push    dx                              ;AN000; save the command name offset
        INT     int_command                     ; Do the EXEC
        pop     dx                              ;AN000; restore the command name offset
        JC      EXEC_ERR                        ; EXEC failed
;
; The exec has completed.  Retrieve the exit code.
;
EXEC_WAIT:
        push    cs                              ;AC000; get resident segment
        pop     ds                              ;AC000;     into DS
        MOV     AH,WAITPROCESS                  ;AC000; Get errorlevel
        INT     int_command                     ; Get the return code
        MOV     [RETCODE],AX

This is the only place that sets RETCODE. Internal commands (COPY, ECHO, DEL, IF …) never change it, and a command that is not found leaves it alone too: "Bad command or file name" is printed on standard error (TMISC1.ASM lines 354-360), and the old value survives. A batch file reads RETCODE with IF ERRORLEVEL n:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.11 – IF ERRORLEVEL n means "exit code >= n", with n taken modulo 256 (TBATCH2.ASM lines 407-435)Source ↗
IFERLEV:
        MOV     BH,10
        XOR     BL,BL

GETNUMLP:
        LODSB
        CMP     AL,0DH
        jz      iferrorj3
        invoke  DELIM
        JZ      GOTNUM
        SUB     AL,'0'
        XCHG    AL,BL
        MUL     BH
        ADD     AL,BL
        XCHG    AL,BL
        JMP     SHORT GETNUMLP

GOTNUM:
        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,[RESSEG]
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP
        MOV     AH,BYTE PTR [RETCODE]
        POP     DS
ASSUME  DS:TRANGROUP
        XOR     AL,AL
        CMP     AH,BL
        JAE     IFRET
        DEC     AL
        JMP     SHORT IFRET

Three facts follow from this code. The test is JAE, "greater than or equal", so a batch file must test the largest value first. Only the low byte of RETCODE is compared, so the exit type in AH is invisible: when DOS stops a program for Ctrl-C (or a divide overflow) it fakes a function 4Ch call with AL = 0 (CTRLC.ASM lines 343-346), so an interrupted program looks exactly like one that succeeded. And the number after ERRORLEVEL is accumulated in an 8-bit register without any check, so IF ERRORLEVEL 300 is IF ERRORLEVEL 44 (300 - 256), and a non-digit is silently "converted" too. labs/09-toolsmith/dos contains RC.ASM, a 36-byte .COM program that exits with the number on its command line, and EXITDEMO.BAT, which tries each case:

Output 9.2 – COMMAND /C EXITDEMO (MS-DOS 4.00; RC.COM built with nasm -f bin)
after RC 44:  IF ERRORLEVEL 44 is true
after RC 44:  IF NOT ERRORLEVEL 45 is true
after RC 44:  IF ERRORLEVEL 300 is true
an internal command
after ECHO:   ERRORLEVEL is still 44 or more
after RC 300: IF ERRORLEVEL 44 is true
after NOSUCH: ERRORLEVEL is still 44 or more
after RC 0:   IF NOT ERRORLEVEL 1 is true

RC 300 computes 300 in 16 bits but can pass only AL, 2Ch = 44, to DOS. The "Bad command or file name" message for NOSUCH is missing from the output because dos_run.py captures only standard output.

On FreeBSD, exit(3) flushes the C streams and calls _exit(2); the system call stores the full int (Table 9.1). When the parent's wait4 collects the child, the kernel packs the low 8 bits of the code and the number of the signal that killed the child, if any, into one status word:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.12 – Only 8 bits of the exit code reach the parent (wait.h lines 140-147)Source ↗
#if defined(_KERNEL) || defined(_WANT_KW_EXITCODE)

/*
 * Clamp the return code to the low 8 bits from full 32 bit value.
 * Should be used in kernel to construct the wait(2)-compatible process
 * status to usermode.
 */
#define KW_EXITCODE(ret, sig)   W_EXITCODE((ret) & 0xff, (sig))

W_EXITCODE is (ret) << 8 | (sig), and WEXITSTATUS shifts it back (wait.h lines 58-63). The layout is the mirror image of DOS's: DOS puts the code in the low byte and the reason in the high byte; FreeBSD puts the code in the high byte and the signal in the low byte. sh turns the status into $?:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.13 – sh converts a wait status to $? (jobs.c lines 1102-1113)Source ↗
        status = getjobstatus(jp);
        if (signaled != NULL)
                *signaled = WIFSIGNALED(status);
        /* convert to 8 bits */
        if (WIFEXITED(status))
                st = WEXITSTATUS(status);
#if JOBS
        else if (WIFSTOPPED(status))
                st = WSTOPSIG(status) + 128;
#endif
        else
                st = WTERMSIG(status) + 128;

Unlike RETCODE, $? is set by every command, builtins included, and a command that cannot be found sets it to 127. exitdemo.sh and status.c in labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd show both levels:

Output 9.3 – sh exitdemo.sh, then ./status N for several N (captured in the course VM)
after exit 44:        $? = 44
after exit 300:       $? = 44
after kill -TERM:     $? = 143
after false:          $? = 1
after echo:           $? = 0
after nosuch:         $? = 127
after [ 1 -gt 2 ]:    $? = 1
else branch, $? = 3
status 0x2c00: exited, WEXITSTATUS = 44
status 0x2c00: exited, WEXITSTATUS = 44
status 0x000f: killed by signal 15
status 0x0000: exited, WEXITSTATUS = 0
Terminated

(Terminated is sh's report, on standard error, about the child it killed; the capture collects standard error separately and appends it.) exit 300 gives 44 on both systems, for the same reason: only 8 bits travel. Figure 9.5 shows the two paths, and Table 9.3 the conventions that tools and scripts build on them.

Table 9.3 – Exit code conventions

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Success 0 0, and if, &&, `
How a script tests IF ERRORLEVEL n (>= n): test the largest value first; IF NOT ERRORLEVEL 1 means "is 0" $?, if cmd, case $? in
Set by external programs only every command, builtins included
Command not found message on standard error, ERRORLEVEL unchanged 127 (126 if found but not executable)
Killed Ctrl-C: code 0, type 1 in AH, invisible to IF ERRORLEVEL 128 + signal number
Values above 255 low byte only (AL) low byte only (& 0xff)
A script's own code none: the last external program's code is what the caller sees (Lab 9.7) exit n, or the status of the last command

The table also explains a habit of DOS utilities: many of them return 0 no matter what, because nobody could rely on exit codes anyway. FIND documents "0 - OK, and some matches" in its header and leaves 1 blank (FIND.ASM lines 37-41), but the only values its code ever stores in the errlevel byte are 0 and, when the command line itself is wrong, 2 (FIND.ASM line 1592). So "no line matched" also returns 0, and so does a file that cannot be opened: FIND prints "File not found", goes on with the next name and finally stores 0 (FIND.ASM lines 955-965). Lab 9.7 finds the same kind of gap in XCOPY. FC is better: it calls exit(1) when the files differ or cannot be opened, and usage(NoDif, 0) when they are equal (FC.C lines 468-473).

9.5 Memory limits#

A .COM program is a memory image with no header, so DOS cannot know how much memory it needs and gives it all: EXEC allocates the largest free block (EXEC.ASM lines 558-568), reads at most 64 KB minus the PSP, and puts the stack at the end of what it could have read:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.14 – The initial registers of a .COM program (EXEC.ASM lines 597-612)Source ↗
        CMP     AX,SI                   ; did we read them all?
        JZ      exec_no_memj            ; exactly the wrong number... no memory
        TEST    BYTE PTR exec_func,exec_func_overlay
        JNZ     exec_set_PDB            ; no starto, chumo!
        MOV     AX,exec_DMA
        SUB     AX,10h
        MOV     exec_init_CS,AX
        MOV     exec_init_IP,100h       ; initial IP is 100
;
; SI is at most FF00h.  Add FE to account for PSP - word of 0 on stack.
;
        ADD     SI,0FEh                 ; make room for stack
        MOV     exec_init_SP,SI         ; max value for read is also SP!
        MOV     exec_init_SS,AX
        MOV     DS,AX
        MOV     WORD PTR [SI],0         ; 0 for return

With 64 KB or more free, SI is FF00h and SP becomes FFFEh, with a zero word on the stack so that a final RET jumps to PSP:0000, where an INT 20h instruction ends the program. If the file fills the whole read (65,280 bytes or more), EXEC fails with "insufficient memory": a .COM file must be smaller than 64 KB minus 256 bytes. Code, data and stack share one segment. The tools in this module need a few hundred bytes of code, a buffer and a little stack, so the limit never bites; but a .COM program that wants to start another program must first give memory back with function 4Ah, because it owns all of it.

A C program in the small model has one code segment and one data segment (DGROUP) of up to 64 KB each; the stack and the near heap live in DGROUP, and the start-up code shrinks the program's block to what it needs (Module 5, sections 5.3 and 5.5). Module 8 measured what that leaves for malloc (Lab 8.4), and its Exercise 8.2 builds a full memory report; SYSINFO (Lab 9.5) only prints the largest free block. The limit that matters most for the C tools here is the size of int: 16 bits in Microsoft C 5.10, so a WC that counts bytes in an int is wrong for any file over 32,767 bytes. All counters in this module's DOS tools are unsigned long, or 32-bit pairs of registers in assembly.

FreeBSD tools live in a private virtual address space of many terabytes, with limits set per process by setrlimit(2). The arguments may total 512 KB (Table 9.1), four thousand times the 127 bytes of a DOS command line, which is why sh can expand *.txt in a directory of thousands of files and COMMAND.COM cannot even try:

Output 9.4 – Limits of a FreeBSD process (captured in the course VM)
# getconf ARG_MAX
524288
# limits | head -12
Resource limits (current):
  cputime              infinity secs
  filesize             infinity kB
  datasize             33554432 kB
  stacksize              524288 kB
  coredumpsize         infinity kB
  memoryuse            infinity kB
  memorylocked         infinity kB
  maxprocesses             6656
  openfiles               57870
  sbsize               infinity bytes
  vmemoryuse           infinity kB

A 32 GB data limit and a 512 MB stack limit on a VM with 2 GB of RAM are not promises; they are ceilings for address space that will be backed by real pages only when touched (Module 8). For a tool that reads a stream through a fixed buffer, as WC and HD do on both systems, the size of the input does not matter at all; only the counters must be wide enough.

9.6 The six tools#

The labs build six tools, each one for a different part of the interface between a program and its system. ARGS shows how the arguments arrive. WC reads standard input or named files and must count past 32,767. HD shows the bytes that text mode hides. SYSINFO asks the system about itself. ASK turns a key into an exit code. BACKUP is a script that glues other programs together and has to trust their exit codes. Table 9.4 shows which versions exist and how each was built. Every cell was built and run on the system named in its column: MS-DOS 4.00 through dos_run.py, FreeBSD 15.1 in the course VM. A dash means that the combination teaches nothing new. SYSINFO in FreeBSD assembly would only call the same library routines, and ASK in C would be the assembly version with a heavier start-up.

Table 9.4 – The tool matrix: MS-DOS 4.00 / FreeBSD 15.1 in each cell

Tool Labs Assembly C Script
ARGS 9.1, 9.2 ARGS.COM (NASM) / argsa (nasm, ld) ARGS.EXE, ARGSW.EXE with SETARGV (CL) / args (cc) – / –
WC 9.3 WCA.COM, standard input only / wca, the same WC.EXE and the text-mode WCT.EXE / wc, from the same source – / –
HD 9.4 HDA.COM / hda HD.EXE / hd, from the same source – / –
SYSINFO 9.5 SYSINFOA.COM / – SYSINFO.EXE (intdos) / sysinfo – / –
ASK 9.6 ASK.COM (MASM, LINK, EXE2BIN) / – – / – ASKDEMO.BAT calls ASK / ask.sh, askdemo.sh
BACKUP 9.7 – / – – / – BACKUP.BAT with XCOPY, FC, FIND, RC / backup.sh

WC and HD are one C source each. The only differences are the CR LF line ends and an #ifdef MSDOS that calls setmode on MS-DOS. Microsoft C 5.10 defines MSDOS for every compilation (Lab 9.3). Every other tool needs a separate source per system. The two assembly languages share no instruction that talks to the system. And on MS-DOS argv[0] is already the full path of the program, which FreeBSD's args.c has to ask the kernel for.

The sizes tell the same story as section 9.2. The DOS assembly tools are a few hundred bytes of instructions and nothing else. The same tools in C are 7 to 10 KB, mostly printf and the start-up code that LINK copies from SLIBCE.LIB into every program (Module 5). On FreeBSD, the assembly tools carry an ELF header, program headers, a symbol table and section names: strip takes argsa from 2,176 to 960 bytes (Lab 9.1). The C tools are 10 to 12 KB even though printf stays in libc.so.7, because they contain the start-up objects and the tables for the run-time linker:

Table 9.5 – Sizes of the built tools, in bytes

Tool MS-DOS, assembly MS-DOS, C FreeBSD, assembly FreeBSD, C
ARGS 251 7,287 (8,407 with SETARGV) 2,176 9,984
WC 215 10,537 2,136 11,528
HD 254 9,721 2,384 12,048
SYSINFO 428 7,735 – 11,176
ASK 377 – – ask.sh: 1,186
BACKUP – – – BACKUP.BAT: 1,514; backup.sh: 989

Conventions. All tools follow the same few rules, so that scripts can use them:

  • Results go to standard output, messages to standard error, in the form wc: nosuch: cannot open. On MS-DOS a message on standard error stays on the screen even when the output is redirected (section 9.1).
  • A tool without a file name reads standard input, so it works in a pipe and under < on both systems. The assembly versions of WC and HD read only standard input.
  • Exit code 0 means success, 1 means that something failed (a file that cannot be opened, a read error, a copy that failed) and 2 means wrong usage. ASK is the exception, because its codes are its answers: 1 for the first key, 2 for the second and so on, 0 for "no answer" and 255 for wrong usage.
  • HD and WC count bytes, not characters: HD opens files in binary mode, and WC reads standard input in binary mode too, so the counts are the same on both systems (section 9.3).
  • On MS-DOS the assembly version gets an A at the end of its name (WCA, HDA, SYSINFOA) and lives next to the C version in the same directory. ARGS is the exception: ARGS.COM and ARGS.EXE differ only in their extension, and you must type ARGS.EXE to run the second one. On FreeBSD the assembly versions are argsa, wca and hda.

The files. labs/09-toolsmith has one directory per system. DOS files have 8.3 names and CR LF line ends; FreeBSD files have LF. Copy the files you need to a work directory before you build. Some test files have a CR LF and a LF version, because a test file must be in the format of the system that reads it:

Labs#

Lab 9.1: ARGS in assembly#

Goal. Find the command line where each kernel leaves it, with no start-up code in between: the command tail in the PSP and the program's path after the environment on MS-DOS, the vectors that execve builds on the stack and the auxiliary vector on FreeBSD. Then compare what the two programs receive for the same typed line.

What you need. labs/09-toolsmith/dos/ARGS.ASM and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/args.asm: two starters whose output helpers (puts, putdec, write) are complete and whose argument handling is left as two TODOs each. labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/rsprdi.asm is complete. NASM on the host and in the VM, the lab disk and the VM. Section 9.1 has the layouts; Module 4 has the instructions.

Steps.

  1. MS-DOS. Complete the two TODOs of Example 9.1: TODO 1 walks the environment block (its segment is the word at PSP:2Ch) to the path that EXEC stored after it; TODO 2 splits the tail at PSP:81h into words. Assemble on the host and run five command lines. The second one contains two blanks between one and two and a tab between two and three (write it as `t inside a double-quoted PowerShell string); the third one redirects the output to a file, which the fourth one displays.

    Terminal
    $ nasm -f bin -o ARGS.COM ARGS.ASM
$ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 120 --file A:\ARGS.COM=ARGS.COM "ARGS" "ARGS one  two`tthree" "ARGS /x:1 *.TXT >OUT.TXT" "TYPE OUT.TXT" "ARGS ""two words"" x"

  2. FreeBSD. Complete the TODOs of args.asm, copy it and poem.txt to ~/lab/09 in the VM, and build it as argsa (the C version of Lab 9.2 will be args):

    Shell
    nasm -f elf64 args.asm && ld -o argsa args.o
./argsa
./argsa one "two words"   *.txt
cd /tmp && ../root/lab/09/argsa; cd ~/lab/09
ls -l argsa && size argsa && strip -o argss argsa && ls -l argss

  3. Does rsp point at argc? rsprdi.asm exits with the difference between rdi and rsp at its entry point. Run it eight times with stack randomization on (the default) and eight times with it off:

    Shell
    nasm -f elf64 rsprdi.asm && ld -o rsprdi rsprdi.o
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do ./rsprdi; printf "%s " $?; done; echo
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do proccontrol -m aslr -s disable ./rsprdi; printf "%s " $?; done; echo
Example 9.1 – The two TODOs of the MS-DOS starter (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/dos/ARGS.ASM)
; Word 0: the path DOS stored after the environment (DOS 3.0 and later).
; TODO 1: print "0: [" with  call number  (argno is still 0).
;         Load DS from the environment segment at PSP offset 2Ch (push DS
;         first), skip every NAME=value string up to the empty string that
;         ends the environment, skip the 0 and the word count that follows,
;         print the path with  call puts , restore DS and print s_close.

; Words 1..n: runs of characters separated by blanks or tabs, up to the CR.
; TODO 2: walk the tail from offset 81h with LODSB.  Skip blanks and tabs;
;         stop at the CR (13).  For each word: remember its first byte in DX,
;         find the delimiter, increment [argno], call number, put the
;         length in CX, call write, print s_close, and continue.

done:   mov     ax, 4C00h               ; exit code 0
        int     21h

The FreeBSD starter gets its only pointer from the kernel's rdi (Listing 9.3) and keeps it in r12, because syscall destroys rcx and r11 and the helpers use rax, rcx, rdx, rsi and rdi:

Example 9.2 – The entry point of the FreeBSD starter (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/args.asm)
_start:
        mov     r12, rdi                ; the kernel's rdi points at argc
        mov     rbx, [r12]              ; rbx = argc
        lea     rsi, [rel s_argc]       ; "argc: "
        call    puts
        mov     rax, rbx
        call    putdec
        lea     rsi, [rel s_nl]
        call    puts

    264       0      21     285     11d argsa
-rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel 960 Nov  9 11:17 argss

0 0 8 0 8 8 8 0
# for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do proccontrol -m aslr -s disable ./rsprdi; printf "%s " $?; done; echo
8 8 8 8 8 8 8 8

What is going on. COMMAND.COM hands over the text after the command name exactly as typed: the leading blank, the two blanks and the tab are all in the 15 bytes, and the CR that ends the tail is not counted. The redirection is different. COMMAND.COM removed >OUT.TXT before it built the tail, so the program never saw it, but the blank that preceded > stayed, which is why the third tail is 12 bytes with a blank at the end. ARGS.COM wrote to handle 1 as always and did not know that the handle now led to a file. Quotes mean nothing to COMMAND.COM or to the kernel, so "two and words" are two words; *.TXT arrives as three characters, and /x:1 is just another word: a switch is a convention that each program parses for itself. Word 0 is the full path that COMMAND.COM found on its search (section 9.2) and that EXEC copied after the environment (Module 3, section 3.7), so the program learns its own name even though it is not in the tail.

On FreeBSD the program receives finished words. The shell collapsed the blanks, removed the quotes and replaced *.txt by the one matching name before execve, and the kernel copied the four strings to the stack (Listing 9.2). argv[0] is whatever the shell passed, here the path as typed (./argsa, ../root/lab/09/argsa). The absolute path comes from the kernel in the auxiliary vector (AT_EXECPATH, section 9.1), which is what a program should use to find files installed next to itself.

The sizes say where the bytes go. ARGS.COM is 251 bytes, all code and strings, because a .COM file has no header at all (Module 5). argsa has 264 bytes of code and read-only data and 21 bytes of .bss, but the file is 2,176 bytes: the ELF header, the program headers that tell the kernel what to map, the section headers and the symbol table. strip removes the symbols and leaves 960 bytes, still almost four times ARGS.COM.

Step 3 explains why the starter takes argc from rdi. With stack randomization on, the kernel moves the top of the stack by a random multiple of 8 bytes inside the first page:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.15 – The top of the new stack moves by a random multiple of 8 (kern_exec.c lines 1269-1274)Source ↗
        stack_top = stack_addr + ssiz;
        if ((map->flags & MAP_ASLR_STACK) != 0) {
                /* Randomize within the first page of the stack. */
                arc4rand(&stack_off, sizeof(stack_off), 0);
                stack_top -= rounddown2(stack_off & PAGE_MASK, sizeof(void *));
        }

The strings and vectors are built below that top, so argc lands on an address that is a multiple of 16 in some runs and not in others, and the rounding of Listing 9.3 then puts rsp either on argc or 8 bytes below it. A program that reads argc from [rsp] works in about half of the runs. Without randomization (proccontrol -m aslr -s disable) the result is the same every time, but it still depends on the length of the strings above, so it is not something to rely on either. MS-DOS has no such question: the tail is always at offset 80h of the segment in which the program starts.

Questions.

  1. Why is the tail of ARGS /x:1 *.TXT >OUT.TXT 12 bytes and not 11? Predict the tail of ARGS >OUT.TXT one and check it.
  2. The tail has room for 127 bytes. Where does ARGS.COM get the length, and what would go wrong if it searched for the CR without using the length byte at all?
  3. argc is a 64-bit word on FreeBSD/amd64. Which instruction of Example 9.2 would you change to read only 32 bits, and why does it not matter here?
  4. Started from /tmp, argsa printed different things for argv[0] and for the path. Name one program in the base system that behaves differently depending on argv[0] (look at ls -li /bin for files with the same inode number).

Lab 9.2: ARGS in C, and who expands the wildcards#

Goal. Let the C start-up code split the command line, and find out who expands *.TXT: the shell on FreeBSD, the program itself on MS-DOS, and then only if it was linked with the right object file.

What you need. labs/09-toolsmith/dos/ARGS.C and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/args.c (each with a TODO: the loop over argv, and on FreeBSD the call to elf_aux_info(3)), the Microsoft C 5.10 toolchain through tools/dos_tools.py (Module 5), POEM.TXT and CTRLZ.TXT from labs/09-toolsmith/dos, and the VM.

Steps.

  1. Complete ARGS.C and build it twice in a work directory: once as it is, and once linked with SETARGV.OBJ, the start-up module that expands wildcards. /link /NOE tells LINK not to use the library's extended dictionary; without it the build stops with error L2044: __setargv : symbol multiply defined, use /NOE, because the library's own _setargv is pulled in as well:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work --timeout 300 "CL /AS ARGS.C" "CL /AS /FeARGSW.EXE ARGS.C T:\BLD\LIB\SETARGV.OBJ /link /NOE"

  2. Run both versions. Type ARGS.EXE with its extension: plain ARGS would start ARGS.COM from Lab 9.1 if it is still on the disk, because COMMAND.COM tries .COM before .EXE (section 9.2). The last two commands add files in a known order so that you can see the order of the expansion:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 120 --file A:\ARGS.EXE=work\ARGS.EXE --file A:\ARGSW.EXE=work\ARGSW.EXE --file A:\POEM.TXT=POEM.TXT --file A:\CTRLZ.TXT=CTRLZ.TXT "ARGS.EXE ""two words"" x" "ARGS.EXE *.TXT /x:1" "ARGSW *.BAS" "COPY POEM.TXT ZZ.TXT" "COPY POEM.TXT AA.TXT" "DIR *.TXT" "ARGSW *.TXT" "ARGSW ""*.TXT"" x" "ARGSW poem.txt C*.*"

  3. FreeBSD. Complete args.c, build it and run it with the same kinds of argument. nick is a second name for the same file:

    Shell
    cc -Wall -o args args.c && ls -l args
./args one "two words" *.txt
./args '*.txt' *.bas
ln -s args nick && ./nick x
ldd args

        libc.so.7 => /lib/libc.so.7 (0x38e948dfd000)
        libsys.so.7 => /lib/libsys.so.7 (0x38e949d64000)
        [vdso] (0x38e9478bd000)

What is going on. The C start-up code of Microsoft C 5.10 does for ARGS.EXE what ARGS.COM did by hand, plus one thing: it treats a double-quoted string as one word and removes the quotes. It does not touch *.TXT. Linked with SETARGV.OBJ, the start-up code also looks for * and ? in each word and replaces a word that matches files by the matching names, in upper case as they are stored in the directory, and sorted: DIR lists the four files in the order of their directory entries, ARGSW in alphabetical order. A word that matches nothing (*.BAS), a word without wildcards (poem.txt) and a quoted word stay as they are. These are the rules of sh (POSIX Shell Command Language, sections 2.6.6 and 2.13: sorted matches, the pattern itself when nothing matches, no expansion inside quotes), reproduced inside one program.

The difference is who applies them. On FreeBSD every program gets the same expansion because the shell does it once, before execve; a program cannot even tell whether its user typed *.txt or the names. On MS-DOS each program decides. ARGS.EXE and ARGSW.EXE are built from the same source and disagree, DIR and COPY are COMMAND.COM's own code and expand *.TXT themselves, and a program built without SETARGV.OBJ that receives *.TXT will try to open a file called *.TXT. That is why a DOS tool's manual must say whether it accepts wildcards, and why BACKUP.BAT in Lab 9.7 hands its patterns to FOR, which expands them.

The path in the auxiliary vector is the file that the kernel actually opened: nick is a symbolic link, so argv[0] says ./nick while AT_EXECPATH says /root/lab/09/args. A program that wants to behave differently under different names (Question 4 of Lab 9.1) must look at argv[0]. The C version is 9,984 bytes against 7,287 on MS-DOS even though it has more to do, because printf lives in the shared library libc.so.7 that ldd lists, while LINK copied printf and everything it needs from SLIBCE.LIB into ARGS.EXE (Module 5).

Questions.

  1. Write a command line for which ARGS.COM and ARGS.EXE report a different number of words, other than one with double quotes.
  2. ARGSW *.TXT sorted the names. Is sorting a property of the file system, of INT 21h function 4Eh, or of the start-up code? Which output of this lab tells you?
  3. ./args '*.txt' and ARGSW "*.TXT" both print the pattern. Give a case in which the two systems still behave differently for the same quoted pattern and the same files. (Hint: what does each program that receives *.TXT do with it?)
  4. On FreeBSD, ls * in a directory with 100,000 files can fail with "Argument list too long". Why can that never happen to ARGSW *.* on MS-DOS, and what can go wrong there instead? (Section 9.5 has both limits.)

Lab 9.3: WC: counting lines, words and bytes#

Goal. Write one C program that builds unchanged on both systems and gives the same counts as FreeBSD's /usr/bin/wc, write a standard-input-only version in assembly for each system, and see what the text mode of the MS-DOS C runtime would have done to the counts.

What you need. labs/09-toolsmith/dos/WC.C and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/wc.c (the same starter, with CR LF and with LF line endings), labs/09-toolsmith/dos/WCA.ASM and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/wca.asm (the read loop and the output are complete; the counting is a TODO), the test files POEM.TXT (six lines, CR LF, 155 bytes) and CTRLZ.TXT from labs/09-toolsmith/dos, and poem.txt (the same poem with LF, 149 bytes) from labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd.

Steps.

  1. Complete the counting loop of WC.C. The rules are those of section 9.3: a LF ends a line, a word is a run of bytes other than blank, tab, LF, VT, FF and CR, and every byte counts. The only system-dependent part is already in the starter:

    Example 9.3 – The one #ifdef of WC.C (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/dos/WC.C)
    #ifdef MSDOS
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <io.h>
#define BINARY_STDIN()  setmode(fileno(stdin), O_BINARY)
#else
#define BINARY_STDIN()
#endif

    Files are opened with fopen(name, "rb"), which is binary on MS-DOS and the same as "r" on FreeBSD. Standard input is already open when main starts, in text mode on MS-DOS, so WC.C switches it with setmode (section 9.3). Build WC.EXE with SETARGV.OBJ so that WC *.TXT works as on FreeBSD (Lab 9.2), and build it a second time as WCT.EXE with /UMSDOS, which removes the predefined MSDOS macro and with it the setmode call:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work --timeout 300 "CL /AS WC.C T:\BLD\LIB\SETARGV.OBJ /link /NOE" "CL /AS /UMSDOS /FeWCT.EXE WC.C T:\BLD\LIB\SETARGV.OBJ /link /NOE"

  2. Complete WCA.ASM. It reads handle 0 in blocks of 512 bytes with function 3Fh and keeps three 32-bit counters, because 16 bits cannot count past 65,535 bytes; put32 prints them. Assemble it on the host with nasm -f bin -o WCA.COM WCA.ASM.

  3. Run both on MS-DOS, on files, on redirected input and at the end of a pipe. WCT is the text-mode build:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 150 --file A:\WC.EXE=work\WC.EXE --file A:\WCT.EXE=work\WCT.EXE --file A:\WCA.COM=WCA.COM --file A:\POEM.TXT=POEM.TXT --file A:\CTRLZ.TXT=CTRLZ.TXT "WC POEM.TXT" "WC *.TXT" "WC <POEM.TXT" "WCA <POEM.TXT" "TYPE POEM.TXT | WCA" "WC <CTRLZ.TXT" "TYPE CTRLZ.TXT | WCA" "WCT <POEM.TXT" "WCT <CTRLZ.TXT" "WCT CTRLZ.TXT" "WC COMMAND.COM" "WCA <COMMAND.COM" "WCA <NUL" "WC POEM.TXT NOSUCH.TXT" "IF ERRORLEVEL 1 ECHO exit code 1 or more"

  4. FreeBSD. Copy wc.c, wca.asm, poem.txt, POEM.TXT and CTRLZ.TXT to ~/lab/09, complete wca.asm (it reads 4,096 bytes at a time and uses 64-bit counters), build both and compare them with the system's wc:

    Shell
    cc -Wall -o wc wc.c && nasm -f elf64 wca.asm && ld -o wca wca.o && ls -l wc wca
./wc poem.txt POEM.TXT CTRLZ.TXT; /usr/bin/wc poem.txt POEM.TXT CTRLZ.TXT
./wca < POEM.TXT; cat poem.txt | ./wca; ./wc < CTRLZ.TXT
./wc nosuch poem.txt; echo "status $?"
./wca < /tmp; echo "status $?"
./wca < /nonexistent-dir; echo "status $?"

  5. Count the read system calls of the three programs on a larger file, /usr/share/dict/web2 (2,494,059 bytes):

    Shell
    truss -o w1.tr ./wc /usr/share/dict/web2 >/dev/null; grep -c "^read(" w1.tr
truss -o w2.tr ./wca < /usr/share/dict/web2 >/dev/null; grep -c "^read(" w2.tr
truss -o w3.tr /usr/bin/wc /usr/share/dict/web2 >/dev/null; grep -c "^read(" w3.tr

What is going on. The same source gives the same numbers on both systems, and the same numbers as FreeBSD's wc, because all three count bytes and treat CR as one more blank. POEM.TXT and poem.txt have the same lines and words; the six extra bytes of the MS-DOS file are its six CRs. The Ctrl-Z in CTRLZ.TXT is an ordinary byte for WC: it counts towards the 39 bytes, and since it is not a blank it is the first byte of the word after.

The other rows show who else touches the bytes. TYPE stops at the Ctrl-Z (section 9.3), so the end of the pipe sees only the 20 bytes before it, two lines and four words. WCT is the same program without the setmode call: its standard input is in text mode, so the C runtime removed the six CRs of POEM.TXT (149 bytes, as on FreeBSD) and stopped reading CTRLZ.TXT at the Ctrl-Z, after 18 bytes instead of the 20 that TYPE passed on. That also proves that Microsoft C 5.10 predefines MSDOS: undefining it changed the result. WCT CTRLZ.TXT opens the file itself with "rb" and counts all 39 bytes, so the text mode of a stream is fixed when it is opened, not by the kind of file behind it.

WCA <NUL reads the NUL device, which returns 0 bytes at once, so all counters stay 0. WC POEM.TXT NOSUCH.TXT counted what it could, printed its message on handle 2, which dos_run.py cannot capture because COMMAND.COM cannot redirect it (section 9.1), and returned 1, which IF ERRORLEVEL 1 saw. On FreeBSD the same message appears in the captured output because bsd_run.py collects descriptor 2 as well, and $? is 1.

The three FreeBSD error cases end differently. wc nosuch is the program's own decision. wca < /tmp started, and its first read failed (EISDIR). A FreeBSD system call reports an error the way an INT 21h function does (Module 4): with the carry flag set and the error number in the accumulator:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.16 – How a system call returns success or an error on amd64 (vm_machdep.c lines 545-581)Source ↗
cpu_set_syscall_retval(struct thread *td, int error)
{
        struct trapframe *frame;

        frame = td->td_frame;
        if (__predict_true(error == 0)) {
                frame->tf_rax = td->td_retval[0];
                frame->tf_rdx = td->td_retval[1];
                frame->tf_rflags &= ~PSL_C;
                return;
        }
⋮
        default:
                frame->tf_rax = error;
                frame->tf_rflags |= PSL_C;

So jc .error took the branch and the program exited with 1. The C library's read does the same test and moves rax to errno. wca < /nonexistent-dir never started: the shell could not open the file for the redirection, printed the message itself and set $? to 2.

Step 5 counts system calls. wca reads 4,096 bytes at a time: 609 full or partial reads plus the one that returns 0. Our C wc reads through stdio, which sized its buffer from the file's st_blksize (32,768 bytes here): 78 reads of the file plus two by the run-time linker before it loads libc.so.7: it reads /etc/libmap.conf (libmap.c line 133) and the header of its hints file /var/run/ld-elf.so.hints (rtld.c line 2149). /usr/bin/wc reads with read(2) into a static buffer of MAXBSIZE bytes (wc.c line 205), 65,536 (param.h line 292), and needs about half as many. It also prints the counts so far, on standard error, when you press Ctrl-T, which sends SIGINFO (wc.c lines 296-298). The MS-DOS C library has much smaller buffers:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.17 – The default buffer size of the Microsoft C 5.10 stdio (STDIO.H lines 33-37)Source ↗
/* buffered I/O macros */

#define  BUFSIZ  512
#define  _NFILE  20
#define  EOF     (-1)

512 bytes is one sector of the disks of the time, and _NFILE is 20, the size of the Job File Table in the PSP (Table 9.1): the library could not use more streams than DOS gives a process handles. WCA uses the same block size.

Questions.

  1. For POEM.TXT, WCT counts as many bytes fewer than WC as the file has lines. Make a file without a Ctrl-Z for which this rule fails, and show with HD and HD -t what text mode removed. Can a file without a Ctrl-Z make the two programs disagree about the number of words? (Hint: what does text mode do with a CR that is not followed by a LF, and which bytes does WC treat as blanks?)
  2. WCA keeps inw across blocks. Give a file of 513 bytes that would be counted wrongly if inw were reset at the start of each block.
  3. WC.C uses unsigned long. What would WC COMMAND.COM print if c were an int in Microsoft C 5.10? And in FreeBSD's cc?
  4. Why does ./wca < /nonexistent-dir exit with status 2 and not 1? Which program decided the 2? Try the same with WCA <NOSUCH.TXT on MS-DOS: what is printed, and what is ERRORLEVEL afterwards?

Lab 9.4: HD: a hex dump, and why binary mode matters#

Goal. Write a hex dump that prints exactly what FreeBSD's hd prints, in C for both systems and in assembly for each, and use it to see what the text mode of the MS-DOS C runtime and TYPE do to a file.

What you need. labs/09-toolsmith/dos/HD.C and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/hd.c (the same starter with two TODOs: the format of a line, and how to open the input), labs/09-toolsmith/dos/HDA.ASM and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/hda.asm (the formatting is given; the read loop is a TODO), CTRLZ.TXT, and RC.COM (built from RC.ASM in section 9.4) as a small binary to look at.

Steps.

  1. Complete HD.C. The format is that of hd: an 8-digit hexadecimal offset, 16 bytes in two groups of 8, the printable bytes between bars, and the total length on a last line. HD -t must open the input in text mode ("r", and no setmode for standard input); without -t it uses "rb" and BINARY_STDIN() as WC does. Build with CL /AS HD.C.

  2. Complete the read loop of HDA.ASM. It must collect 16 bytes per line even when one read returns fewer, which happens with the console and, on FreeBSD, with pipes:

    Example 9.4 – The read loop that the assembly starters leave as a TODO (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/dos/HDA.ASM)
    nextln: xor     bp, bp                  ; BP = bytes in this line so far
fill:
; TODO: read the rest of the line (16 - BP bytes) from handle 0 into
;       data + BP with function 3Fh.  On an error go to failed; when 0 bytes
;       come back go to eof; otherwise add them to BP and read again until
;       BP is 16: a pipe or the console may return fewer bytes than asked for.
eof:    or      bp, bp
        jz      finish
        call    putline

  3. Run them on MS-DOS:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 150 --file A:\HD.EXE=work\HD.EXE --file A:\HDA.COM=HDA.COM --file A:\RC.COM=RC.COM --file A:\CTRLZ.TXT=CTRLZ.TXT "HD CTRLZ.TXT" "HD -t CTRLZ.TXT" "HDA <CTRLZ.TXT" "TYPE CTRLZ.TXT | HDA" "HD -t <CTRLZ.TXT" "HD RC.COM" "HD NOSUCH.TXT" "IF ERRORLEVEL 1 ECHO exit code 1 or more" "HDA <NUL"

  4. In the VM, build hd.c and hda.asm, run them on the same file, feed hda through a pipe that delivers 10 bytes, pauses and delivers 10 more, and compare both with the system's hd on a large binary. hd prints * instead of repeated lines; hd -v prints them all, as ours do:

    Shell
    cc -Wall -o hd hd.c && nasm -f elf64 hda.asm && ld -o hda hda.o && ls -l hd hda
./hd CTRLZ.TXT; ./hd -t CTRLZ.TXT; ./hda < CTRLZ.TXT
(printf "0123456789"; sleep 1; printf "abcdefghij") | ./hda
./hda < /bin/sh > a.out; hd -v /bin/sh > b.out; cmp a.out b.out && echo same
./hd /bin/sh | cmp - b.out && echo same; hd /bin/sh | grep -c "^\*"
ls -li /usr/bin/hd /usr/bin/hexdump
sed -n "50,56p" /usr/src/usr.bin/hexdump/hexsyntax.c

            strcmp(p, "hd") == 0) {
                /* "Canonical" format, implies -C. */
                add("\"%08.8_Ax\n\"");

What is going on. In binary mode the dump shows the file as it is on the disk: 39 bytes, each line ending in 0d 0a, the Ctrl-Z (1a) at offset 14h, and the third line after it. The same HD.EXE with -t sees 18 bytes: the C runtime turned each CR LF into a LF and reported the end of the file at the Ctrl-Z, although the kernel had more to give. The runtime's source is not part of the MS-DOS tree; this dump is the evidence that its text mode does both things, for a file opened with "r" and for a standard input left in text mode alike. TYPE passes 20 bytes into the pipe: it also stops at the Ctrl-Z (Listing 9.6), but keeps the CRs. Three programs, three answers for the same 39 bytes; only the binary readers agree with the directory entry.

On FreeBSD -t changes nothing, because "r" and "rb" are the same (Listing 9.8): the first two dumps of Output 9.12 are identical. The rest of step 4 tests the parts that are easy to get wrong. The pipe delivered 10 bytes, then 10 more a second later; hda's first read returned 10, and without the loop of Example 9.4 the first line would have had 10 bytes and every later offset would have been wrong. On /bin/sh both our programs produce the same 10,632 lines as hd -v; plain hd replaced repeated lines by * 55 times.

The last two commands answer Question 4 of Lab 9.1. hd is not a program of its own: it is a third name (link count 3, same inode 1966) of hexdump, next to od (Makefile lines 7-8), and hexdump looks at the end of argv[0] (hexsyntax.c lines 50-57). If it is hd, it installs the format of -C, written in hexdump's own format language: %08.8_ax is the offset, 8/1 "%02x " eight bytes, %_p a byte as a printable character or a dot. HD RC.COM shows the code of section 9.4 in the same format: be 81 00 is MOV SI,81h, the start of the tail, and b4 4c cd 21 at the end is MOV AH,4Ch / INT 21h.

Questions.

  1. HD -t CTRLZ.TXT shows 18 bytes. Predict, then check, what it shows for a file that contains a, CR, CR, LF, b. Is the text mode of Microsoft C "CR LF becomes LF" or "CR is removed"?
  2. The FreeBSD hda and hd agree on /bin/sh (170,088 bytes). Would HDA.COM and HD.EXE agree on a file of 100,000 bytes? Look at how each one keeps the offset.
  3. HD.EXE writes its lines with printf("...\n") to a standard output in text mode. What bytes end each line when you redirect it to a file on MS-DOS, and how could you check that with the tools of this module?
  4. Implement the * of hd: print * once for any run of lines equal to the line before them. Which test of step 4 tells you that you did it right?

Lab 9.5: SYSINFO: asking the system about itself#

Goal. Write a program that prints what each system tells a program about itself: its version, the current directory, the free space of the current disk and the memory available. On MS-DOS every answer is one INT 21h function; on FreeBSD the answers come from library functions, system calls and sysctl. Then find out how far the answers can be trusted.

What you need. labs/09-toolsmith/dos/SYSINFO.C (the version and the directory are given; the disk and the memory are TODOs), labs/09-toolsmith/dos/SYSINFOA.ASM (the same program in assembly; the memory query is the TODO) and labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd/sysinfo.c (uname and getcwd are given; statfs, sysctlbyname and getrlimit are the TODO). The memory part is kept small on purpose: Module 8, Exercise 8.2 (MEMINFO) is the full memory report for MS-DOS, and this lab only reuses its central call.

Steps.

  1. Complete SYSINFO.C. Microsoft C's intdos (declared in DOS.H) copies a union REGS into the registers, executes INT 21h and copies the registers back, so each TODO is a few assignments and a printf:

    Example 9.5 – The disk TODO of the C starter (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/dos/SYSINFO.C)
        /* TODO 1: function 36h with DL = 0 returns AX = sectors per cluster (FFFFh
     * for an invalid drive), BX = free clusters, CX = bytes per sector and

What is going on. On MS-DOS each line of output is one or two INT 21h calls: 30h for the version, 19h and 47h for the drive and the directory (47h returns WORK, without the drive and the first backslash, so the program adds A:\ itself), 36h for the disk and 48h for the memory. Function 36h answers in clusters, not bytes: on this 1.44 MB floppy a cluster is one sector of 512 bytes, and 2,847 clusters make the 1,457,664 bytes. MKDIR WORK cost exactly one cluster (267,776 - 267,264 = 512): a directory is a file, and space is handed out a cluster at a time.

The two memory figures differ by 71,088 bytes, and the link map explains them to the byte. Both programs give memory back with function 4Ah when they start (the C start-up code does it for SYSINFO.EXE, Module 5, section 5.5), but they keep different amounts. SYSINFOA keeps 59 paragraphs (944 bytes: the PSP, its 428 bytes and a 256-byte stack). SYSINFO.EXE keeps the PSP, its code (_TEXT is 01860H = 6,240 bytes in SYSINFO.MAP) and a whole 64 KB DGROUP for its data, stack and near heap: 256 + 6,240 + 65,536 = 72,032 bytes, and 72,032 - 944 = 71,088. MEM's "largest executable program size" is 976 bytes larger than SYSINFOA's figure, roughly the size of SYSINFOA's own block.

The surprise is IBMCACHE: the same 428 bytes under another name report MS-DOS 3.40, and the next SYSINFOA is back to 4.00. MS-DOS 4.00 carries a table of programs that were known to refuse a version they did not expect:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.18 – Programs that MS-DOS 4.00 lies to (MSINIT.ASM lines 646-661)Source ↗
;The following entries don't expect version 4.0
;The entry format: name_length, name, expected version, fake count
;fake_count: ff means the version will be reset when Abort or Exec is encountered
;            n means the version will be reset after n DOS version calls are issued
;
Version_Fake_Table:                         ;AN007  starting address for special
        DB      12,"IBMCACHE.COM",3,40,255  ;AN007  ibmcache     1
        DB      12,"IBMCACHE.SYS",3,40,255  ;AN007  ibmcache     2
        DB      12,"DXMA0MOD.SYS",3,40,255  ;AN007  lan support  3
        DB      10,"WIN200.BIN"  ,3,40,4    ;AN008  windows      4
        DB       9,"PSCPG.COM"   ,3,40,255  ;AN008  vittoria     5
        DB      11,"DCJSS02.EXE" ,3,40,255  ;AN008  netview      6
        DB       8,"ISAM.EXE"    ,3,40,255  ;AN008  basic        7
        DB       9,"ISAM2.EXE"   ,3,40,255  ;AN008  basic        8
        DB      12,"DFIA0MOD.SYS",3,40,255  ;AN008  lan support  9
        DB      20  dup(0)                  ;AN007

When EXEC loads a program it compares the file name, without the drive and directory, with each entry (EXEC.ASM lines 862-921); on a match it stores the "expected version" (3 and 40, which function 30h returns as AL = 3, AH = 40) and the fake count. Function 30h then answers from that variable:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.19 – Function 30h returns the fake version while the fake count allows it (GETSET.ASM lines 94-113)Source ↗
        context DS
        MOV     BX,[USERNUM + 2]
        MOV     CX,[USERNUM]
        MOV     AX,[MSVERS]
        invoke  get_user_stack
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        MOV     [SI.user_BX],BX
        MOV     [SI.user_CX],CX
        CMP     CS:[Fake_Count],0FFH               ;AN008;
        JZ      reg                                ;AN008;
        CMP     CS:[Fake_Count],0                  ;AN008;
        JZ      usual                              ;AN008;
        DEC     CS:[Fake_Count]                    ;AN008;
reg:                                               ;AN008;
        CMP     CS:[Special_version],0             ;AN006;
        JZ      usual                              ;AN006;
        MOV     AX,CS:[Special_version]            ;AN006;
usual:                                             ;AN006;
        MOV     [SI.user_AX],AX         ; Really only sets AH
        return

A count of FFh gives the fake version to every call, until Reset_Version clears it. That routine runs at the start of every table lookup in EXEC (EXEC.ASM line 886) and whenever a program ends, because every way to end goes through reset_environment (PROC.ASM line 183; CTRLC.ASM line 636). That is why the SYSINFOA after IBMCACHE is back to 4.00. But Reset_Version clears the fake version only when the count is FFh (EXEC.ASM lines 923-930). Any other count is used up only by calls of function 30h, so what WIN200.BIN leaves of its count carries over: the next programs that ask are told 3.40 too, whatever their names, until the count reaches 0 or a program from the table replaces it.

VER is internal to COMMAND.COM, but it asks the same function 30h (TCMD2A.ASM lines 92-103). It said 4.00 because COMMAND.COM is not in the table and IBMCACHE had ended. MS-DOS 5.0 turned this table into the SETVER command; in 4.00 it is fixed in the kernel, and a program is identified by nothing more than its name.

FreeBSD answers the same questions in a different way. uname is not a system call: truss shows that one call of the library function costs five __sysctl calls, one per field. getcwd is a real system call (__getcwd), and statfs(".") names the file system that holds the directory, /dev/gpt/rootfs mounted on /. /tmp gives the same disk line because it is on the same file system: the question is "which mount holds this directory", not "which drive letter". The numbers are df's: 11,862,524 KB available is 12,147,224,576 bytes. The memory lines show the physical memory of the VM (about 2 GB) and a data size limit of 32 GB, sixteen times as much: a limit is a ceiling on address space, not memory set aside, and ulimit -d in a subshell lowers it for the children of that shell only (section 8.7 of Module 8 sets the same limits in login.conf). The six lines leave the program as one write of 226 bytes, because standard output was a pipe.

The FreeBSD answer can be faked too, but by the caller and not by the kernel:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.20 – uname takes a field from the environment before it asks the kernel (__xuname.c lines 50-65)Source ↗
        mib[0] = CTL_KERN;

        if ((p = getenv("UNAME_s")))
                strlcpy(q, p, namesize);
        else {
                mib[1] = KERN_OSTYPE;
                len = namesize;
                oerrno = errno;
                if (sysctl(mib, 2, q, &len, NULL, 0) == -1) {
                        if (errno == ENOMEM)
                                errno = oerrno;
                        else
                                rval = -1;
                }
                q[namesize - 1] = '\0';
        }

UNAME_s=MS-DOS UNAME_r=3.40 ./sysinfo therefore reports "MS-DOS 3.40 amd64", and the manual page of uname(1) documents the variables. sysctl kern.osrelease asks the kernel directly and is not fooled. Both systems built a way to lie about the version for the same reason, old programs that test it too strictly; MS-DOS keys the lie on the program's name inside the kernel, FreeBSD on an environment variable that the user sets.

Questions.

  1. Function 47h returned WORK for A:\WORK. What does it return in the root directory, and what would SYSINFO print if it did not add the backslash itself? Which FreeBSD function needs no such help?
  2. On the floppy, how much does "bytes free" drop when you create a file of one byte? Predict the answer for FreeBSD, where ls -s shows the space a file uses, and check it with sysinfo.
  3. From SYSINFO.MAP, explain the 71,088 bytes between SYSINFO and SYSINFOA. Would a large-model build (CL /AL) report more or less free memory? (Module 8, Lab 8.4.)
  4. WIN200.BIN has a fake count of 4. From Listing 9.19, how many calls of function 30h get 3.40, and what does the next one get? What does a program that is not in the table get if it runs right after a WIN200.BIN that called function 30h only twice?
  5. Why would a user of FreeBSD set UNAME_r? Think of building software on 15.1 for a machine that runs an older release.

Lab 9.6: ASK: an answer as an exit code#

Goal. MS-DOS 4.00 has no command that reads the keyboard for a batch file (there is no CHOICE in v4.0/src/CMD; it arrived with MS-DOS 6). Write ASK, a program that asks a question and gives the answer back as its exit code, and use it from a batch file. Write the FreeBSD version as a script with read. Then try three ways of answering on each system: the keyboard, a file, and Ctrl-C. Also try running out of input. Here the two systems differ most, and MS-DOS 4.00 hangs in one of the cases.

What you need. In labs/09-toolsmith/dos: ASK.ASM (MASM syntax, two TODOs), ASKDEMO.BAT (one TODO), the answer files Y.ANS, N.ANS, JUNK.ANS ("maybe", then "q") and EMPTY.ANS (0 bytes), and two complete test helpers. STUFF.ASM puts keys into the BIOS keyboard buffer as if they had been typed. CCTEST.ASM types Ctrl-C, runs ASK with EXEC and prints what function 4Dh says about how ASK ended. In labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd: ask.sh, askdemo.sh (one TODO each) and y.ans, n.ans, junk.ans, empty.ans. ASK is written for MASM 5.10 so that this module uses the 1988 toolchain of Module 5 once more: MASM, LINK and EXE2BIN.
