What is going on. Where the answer comes from. A program cannot tell from the command line where its standard input points. COMMAND.COM removed <Y.ANS from the tail (Lab 9.1), but it left the blanks around it, which is why ASK trims blanks at the end of its prompt. So ASK asks DOS. IOCTL function 4400h returns the flags of the handle's SFT; for a device, bit 7 is set and bit 0 means "console input". On the keyboard ASK reads with function 08h: one key, no echo, no Enter, with Ctrl-C checking. A wrong key beeps (the ^G in Output 9.15), and an extended key arrives as 0 followed by its scan code, which ASK reads and rejects. From a file or a pipe, ASK reads one byte at a time with function 3Fh. There, a wrong answer cannot be typed again, so ASK skips to the next line. 0 bytes is the end of the input. JUNK.ANS shows both: with keys YN, "maybe" and "q" are skipped and the file ends (exit code 0); with YNQ the second line is the answer. ask.sh asks the same question with [ -t 0 ]. test calls isatty(0) (test.c line 306), and isatty is nothing but a tcgetattr that succeeds only on a terminal (isatty.c lines 35-43; Module 6). Its read gets a whole line, because the terminal is in canonical mode and the line discipline keeps the characters until Enter. The pseudo-terminal echoed x and n itself; ask.sh echoes the key only when the input is not a terminal.

The exit codes. ASKDEMO.BAT must test 255 first and 1 last, because IF ERRORLEVEL n means "n or more" (Listing 9.11). askdemo.sh uses case $?, which compares exact values, so its order does not matter.

Ctrl-C. CCTEST sets its own Ctrl-C handler (STC, RETF: "abort the program") and puts Ctrl-C in the keyboard buffer before it runs ASK. ASK was stopped before its prompt appeared, because DOS looks for Ctrl-C each time a program writes to a character device (DISK.ASM lines 619-620). At the prompt, function 08h would have found it as well. DOS then ends the program as if it had called function 4Ch with AL = 0 (section 9.4). Function 4Dh tells the parent the truth: exit type 1, "ended by Ctrl-C". But COMMAND.COM keeps only the low byte, so for IF ERRORLEVEL Ctrl-C and "no answer" are both 0. In a batch file, COMMAND.COM's handler first asks "Terminate batch job (Y/N)?" and, on N, lets DOS end the program and continues the batch file (COMMAND1.ASM lines 543-552), so ASKDEMO would print "No answer". This is why there is no STUFF ^Cn test: the question empties the keyboard buffer before it reads (function 0Ch in RUCODE.ASM lines 104-115), so the stuffed n is thrown away and the question waits for ever. On FreeBSD, the Ctrl-C key never reaches the program as a character:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.21 – The terminal turns Ctrl-C into SIGINT for the whole foreground process group (tty_ttydisc.c lines 1115-1134)Source ↗
                signal = 0;
                if (CMP_CC(VINTR, c)) {
                        signal = SIGINT;
                } else if (CMP_CC(VQUIT, c)) {
                        signal = SIGQUIT;
                } else if (CMP_CC(VSUSP, c)) {
                        signal = SIGTSTP;
                }

                if (signal != 0) {
                        /*
                         * Echo the character before signalling the
                         * processes.
                         */
                        if (!CMP_FLAG(l, NOFLSH))
                                tty_flush(tp, FREAD|FWRITE);
                        ttydisc_echo(tp, c, 0);
                        tty_signal_pgrp(tp, signal);
                        return (0);
                }

Both systems echo ^C (DOS in CTRLC.ASM lines 286-288). The difference is the target: the signal goes to the process group, so askdemo.sh dies together with ask.sh and prints nothing. script reports the signal number, 2, as its own exit status (script.c lines 408-422). In the last test the signal came from timeout, not from a terminal: without --foreground it makes itself a reaper and sends SIGINT with procctl(PROC_REAP_KILL) to its own descendants, here ask.sh, and not to a process group (timeout.c lines 167-189). With --preserve-status it then kills itself with the signal that ended its child, to pass the status on (timeout.c lines 486-491), and $? is 130 = 128 + 2 (Listing 9.13). So a FreeBSD script can tell "interrupted" from "no answer"; a DOS batch file cannot.

The hang. The last run of Output 9.16 never ends, although ASK read the same empty file without trouble in Output 9.15. Two experiments narrow it down. A batch file whose first line is HDA (Lab 9.4) dumps Y.ANS and continues. Put REM x before that line and the batch file hangs, as ASKDEMO does. A program that reads redirected input to its end hangs only when an internal command has run before it in the same batch file. The messages show what happened. The read at the end of the file raised a critical error, "Out of input", and COMMAND.COM's critical-error handler asked "Abort, Fail?". It reads the answer from standard input (RUCODE.ASM lines 388-390). That is the same empty file, and for a file the input status is "not ready" at the end (DEV.ASM lines 97-103), so the question waits for a key that can never come.

The error comes from a feature that MS-DOS 4.00 added. Bit 8 of an SFT's flags asks DOS to raise a critical error when a read reaches the end of a file or a write finds the disk full (DISK3.ASM lines 584-623). The message services that 4.00's utilities share contain SETSTDINON and SETSTDINOFF, which set and clear that bit on standard input through IOCTL 4400h and 4401h (MSGSERV.ASM lines 379-426). COMMAND.COM turns the bit on for internal commands and off for external ones:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.22 – COMMAND.COM sets the bit before an internal command and clears it before EXEC (TMISC1.ASM lines 199-322)Source ↗
; All messages get redirected.
;
    cmp     append_exec,0                       ;AN041; APPEND just executed?
    jnz     dont_set_io                         ;AN041; Yes - this junk is already set
    invoke  ioset                               ; re-direct the ol' i/o

dont_set_io:                                    ;AN041;
    invoke  SETSTDINON                          ;AN026; turn on critical error on STDIN
    invoke  SETSTDOUTOFF                        ;AN026; turn off critical error on STDOUT
⋮
EXECUTE:
NeoExecute:
        invoke  IOSET
        invoke  SETSTDINOFF                     ;AN026; turn off critical error on STDIN
        invoke  SETSTDOUTOFF                    ;AN026; turn off critical error on STDOUT

The intent is sound: an internal command that reads past the end should get an error, while an external program should get the usual 0 bytes. But the "off" never works for a file:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.23 – IOCTL 4401h can set bit 8 of a file's flags but never clear it (IOCTL.ASM lines 260-286)Source ↗
ioctl_check_permissions:
        CMP     AL,2
        JAE     ioctl_control_string
        CMP     AL,0
        MOV     AL,BYTE PTR ES:[DI.sf_flags]; Get low byte of flags
        JZ      ioctl_read              ; read the byte
        PUSH    DX                      ;AN000;MS.
        AND     DH,0FEH                 ;AN000;MS.allow DH=01H
        POP     DX                      ;AN000;MS.
        JZ      ioctl_check_device      ; can I set with this data?
        error   error_invalid_data      ; no DH <> 0

ioctl_bad_funj2:
        JMP     ioctl_bad_fun

ioctl_check_device:
        TEST    AL,devid_device         ; can I set this handle?
        JZ      do_exception            ; no, it is a file.
        OR      DL,devid_device         ; Make sure user doesn't turn off the
                                        ;   device bit!! He can muck with the
                                        ;   others at will.
        MOV     [EXTERR_LOCUS],errLOC_SerDev
        MOV     BYTE PTR ES:[DI.sf_flags],DL  ;AC000;MS.; Set flags
do_exception:
        OR      BYTE PTR ES:[DI.sf_flags+1],DH;AN000;MS.;set 100H bit for disk full

        transfer    SYS_RET_OK

For a file, function 4400h returns DH = 0 (only devices get a high byte), so SETSTDINON sends DH = 1 and SETSTDINOFF sends DH = 0, and the OR at do_exception turns 0 into "no change". In the batch file every line shares the one SFT that COMMAND /C ... <EMPTY.ANS opened. @ECHO OFF (or REM) sets the bit, the EXEC of ASK fails to clear it, and ASK's read at the end of the file becomes a critical error. At the command line, or with <file on the batch line itself, every command gets a fresh SFT with the bit clear. That is why Output 9.15 works. There are three ways round the bug. Redirect inside the batch file. Give the program more input than it reads. Or start the batch with COMMAND /F, which answers "Fail" to every critical error (RUCODE.ASM lines 381-386): the read then returns with the carry flag set, ASK treats the error as the end of the input, and ASKDEMO prints "No answer". (With /F, HDA loses its last bytes instead, because it treats the error as an error.) FreeBSD has nothing like this: read returns 0 at the end of a file however often it is called, and ask.sh ends its loop.

Questions.

  1. Why does ASK beep at a wrong key from the keyboard but skip a line from a file? What would happen if it beeped and waited for another byte from JUNK.ANS?
  2. In ASKDEMO.BAT, move IF ERRORLEVEL 1 GOTO YES to the top. Which answers still work? In askdemo.sh, what does reordering the case branches change?
  3. After Ctrl-C at the prompt, what does ASKDEMO.BAT print if the user answers N to "Terminate batch job"? What does askdemo.sh print? Which system lets a script tell "interrupted" from "no answer", and where is the information lost on the other one?
  4. Explain why COMMAND /C ASKDEMO <EMPTY.ANS hangs but ASK YN <EMPTY.ANS does not. Which instruction of Listing 9.23 would have to change, and how, for SETSTDINOFF to work on files?
  5. ask.sh needs Enter. Using stty (Module 6), change it to react to a single key on a terminal, and restore the terminal settings even after Ctrl-C (stty -g and trap).

Lab 9.7: BACKUP: a script that copies only what changed#

Goal. Write the same small backup script for both shells: copy the files that match some patterns into a backup directory, skip the ones that have not changed, report how many were copied, unchanged and failed, and end with an exit code that a calling script can test. The script language has to reach every one of those goals through other programs on MS-DOS, and the lab finds three places where a DOS tool's exit code says less than its messages.

What you need. In labs/09-toolsmith/dos: BACKUP.BAT (three TODOs), EL.BAT (a complete helper that prints the current ERRORLEVEL; run it with CALL), RC.ASM from section 9.4, and the test files of the earlier labs (POEM.TXT, CTRLZ.TXT and the four .ANS files). In labs/09-toolsmith/freebsd: backup.sh (three TODOs), poem.txt and the four .ans files. MS-DOS 4.00 supplies FC, FIND and XCOPY; the script uses no other program than these and RC.COM.

Steps.

  1. Read the main loop of the starter. A FOR line can run only one command, so for each matching file the batch file calls itself with a marker, :ONE, as its first argument; the first line of the file sends such a call to the subroutine. SHIFT moves every parameter down, %0 included (Module 3, section 3.6), so the file's own name is saved in BAKBAT before the first SHIFT. A called copy has its own %1 to %9 but shares the environment, so the backup directory and the failure flag travel in BAKDIR and BAKFAIL:

    Example 9.7 – The main loop and the subroutine's entry (excerpt of labs/09-toolsmith/dos/BACKUP.BAT)
    IF "%1"==":ONE" GOTO ONE
IF "%2"=="" GOTO USAGE
IF NOT EXIST %1\NUL GOTO USAGE
SET BAKBAT=%0
SET BAKDIR=%1
SET BAKFAIL=
TYPE NUL >%1\COPIED.LST
TYPE NUL >%1\SAME.LST
TYPE NUL >%1\FAILED.LST
:NEXT
SHIFT
IF "%1"=="" GOTO DONE
FOR %%F IN (%1) DO CALL %BAKBAT% :ONE %%F
GOTO NEXT

    A batch file cannot add, so the subroutine appends each name to COPIED.LST, SAME.LST or FAILED.LST, and at the end FIND /C /V "?" counts the lines of the three lists (no file name contains a ?).

  2. Complete the TODOs. TODO 1 decides "same": the backup exists and FC /B finds no difference (exit code 0, section 9.4). TODO 2 copies with XCOPY and goes to FAILED if its exit code is 1 or more; the starter's COPY reports "copied" whatever happens. TODO 3 ends the script with RC 1 if anything failed and RC 0 otherwise. A batch file has no exit n (Table 9.3), so the last program it runs supplies its exit code.

  3. Run the tests. BACKUP.BAT is always typed with its extension, because A:\BACKUP.COM (MS-DOS's own backup program) comes first in the search order (Listing 9.4). The first run copies everything and fails on a name that does not exist; the second finds everything unchanged; then one file changes, and then the backup copy of another is made read-only with ATTRIB +R before its original changes:

    Terminal
    $ nasm -f bin -o RC.COM RC.ASM
$ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 240 --file A:\BACKUP.BAT=BACKUP.BAT --file A:\EL.BAT=EL.BAT --file A:\RC.COM=RC.COM --file A:\POEM.TXT=POEM.TXT --file A:\CTRLZ.TXT=CTRLZ.TXT --file A:\Y.ANS=Y.ANS --file A:\N.ANS=N.ANS --file A:\JUNK.ANS=JUNK.ANS --file A:\EMPTY.ANS=EMPTY.ANS "CTTY COM1" "PATH A:\" "MKDIR WORK" "MKDIR SAVE" "COPY *.TXT WORK" "COPY *.ANS WORK" "TYPE NUL >WORK\EMPTY.ANS" "CD WORK" "BACKUP SAVE *.TXT" "CALL A:\EL" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE" "CALL A:\EL" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.TXT *.ANS NOSUCH.DAT" "CALL A:\EL" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.TXT *.ANS" "CALL A:\EL" "ECHO more>>Y.ANS" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.ANS" "CALL A:\EL" "ATTRIB +R A:\SAVE\POEM.TXT" "ECHO extra line>>POEM.TXT" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.TXT" "CALL A:\EL" "TYPE A:\SAVE\FAILED.LST" "RC 0" "COPY POEM.TXT A:\SAVE" "CALL A:\EL" "XCOPY POEM.TXT A:\SAVE" "CALL A:\EL" "XCOPY NOSUCH.DAT A:\SAVE" "CALL A:\EL" "COPY EMPTY.ANS A:\" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.TXT >BAK.LOG" "DIR BAK.LOG" "COMMAND /C A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.TXT >BAK.LOG" "CALL A:\EL" "TYPE BAK.LOG" "FOR %%F IN (A:\*.BAT *.XYZ NOSUCH.XYZ) DO ECHO [%%F]" "CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT A:\SAVE *.XYZ" "CALL A:\EL"

    CTTY COM1 is needed here, not only for the error messages: what a batch file prints does not follow the >COM1 that dos_run.py adds to each command (step 4 shows why). CALL matters too: started without it from AUTOEXEC.BAT, BACKUP.BAT would replace AUTOEXEC.BAT and the run would never reach its end marker (Module 3, section 3.6).

  4. The same run goes on with four experiments: COPY and XCOPY on the read-only file and on a missing one, COPY of the empty file, the script's output redirected to a file in two ways, and FOR with patterns that match nothing.

  5. FreeBSD. Complete backup.sh: TODO 1 is [ -e "$b" ] && ! [ "$f" -nt "$b" ], TODO 2 is cp -p inside an if, TODO 3 makes the last command [ "$failed" -eq 0 ]. Then run the same tests in ~/lab/09/work, with one file name that contains a space, which DOS cannot have. You are root in the VM, and root ignores the permission bits (chmod 444 does not stop its cp), so the read-only test uses the uchg flag of chflags(1) instead, which even root cannot write through:

    Shell
    mkdir work save && cp poem.txt y.ans n.ans junk.ans empty.ans work/ && printf 'one\ntwo\n' > 'work/my notes.txt' && ls work
cd work
sh ../backup.sh ../save 2>&1; echo status $?
sh ../backup.sh ../save *.txt *.ans nosuch.dat 2>&1; echo status $?
sh ../backup.sh ../save *.txt *.ans 2>&1; echo status $?
echo more >> y.ans && sh ../backup.sh ../save *.ans 2>&1; echo status $?
chflags uchg ../save/poem.txt && echo 'extra line' >> poem.txt && sh ../backup.sh ../save *.txt 2>&1; echo status $?
ls -lo ../save/poem.txt
sh ../backup.sh ../save *.dat 2>&1; echo status $?
sh -e ../backup.sh ../save nosuch.dat y.ans 2>&1; echo status $?
sh ../backup.sh ../save *.txt >bak.log 2>&1; echo status $?; cat bak.log
chflags nouchg ../save/poem.txt

What is going on. Both scripts give the same answers for the same files: six copied and one failure, then six unchanged, then the changed answer file, then the file whose backup cannot be written. Both report the failure with exit code 1 and a usage error with 2. What differs is how each script learns what happened.

An exit code for a batch file. IF ERRORLEVEL reads one byte in COMMAND.COM's resident data, the code of the last external program (section 9.4). A batch file has no code of its own, so BACKUP.BAT runs RC 0 or RC 1 as its last program, and whoever called it reads that byte. Plain BACKUP instead runs BACKUP.COM, which says "Invalid drive specification" and leaves 4. Through COMMAND /C the code also leaves the shell: after each command the transient part returns to TCOMMAND, which first restores the standard handles and then, once a /C command (here: the whole batch file) is finished, jumps to $EXIT:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.24 – The top of COMMAND.COM's command loop (excerpt) (TCODE.ASM lines 115-134)Source ↗
TCOMMAND:
⋮
NOSETVER2:
        CALL    [HEADCALL]                      ; Make sure header fixed
        XOR     BP,BP                           ; Flag transient not read
        CMP     [SINGLECOM],-1
        JNZ     COMMAND

$EXITPREP:
        PUSH    CS
        POP     DS
        JMP     $EXIT                           ; Have finished the single command

A batch file started by /C marks SINGLECOM with 0FFF0h so that its lines can run (TBATCH.ASM lines 922-924), and the end of the file sets it back to -1 (TBATCH2.ASM lines 154-156). $EXIT ends the secondary COMMAND.COM with function 4Ch and RetCode, the last program's code (TCMD2B.ASM lines 471-473). That is the "exit code 1" after COMMAND /C A:\BACKUP.BAT in Output 9.19.

Why XCOPY and not COPY. COPY is internal: it prints "Access denied" and "0 File(s) copied" and leaves ERRORLEVEL as it was (0 in Output 9.19, set by RC 0 just before). It has a second surprise. COPY *.ANS WORK listed four names but copied three, and COPY EMPTY.ANS A:\ copied none, because when COPY closes a destination into which it wrote nothing, it deletes it:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.25 – COPY deletes a destination it wrote nothing to (excerpt) (COPY.ASM lines 805-906)Source ↗
        MOV     AX,[WRITTEN]
        ADD     AX,[NXTADD]
        JC      BINCLOS                         ; > 1
        CMP     AX,1
        JZ      FORGETITJ                       ; WRITTEN = 0 NXTADD = 1 (the ^Z)
BINCLOS:
        invoke  TRYFLUSH
        jnz     CONCHNG
        cmp     [WRITTEN],0
ForgetItJ:
        jnz     no_forget                       ;AC000; Wrote something
        jmp     FORGETIT                        ;AC000; Never wrote nothing
⋮
FORGETIT:
        MOV     BX,[DESTHAND]
        CALL    DODCLOSE                        ; Close the dest
        call    DestDelete
        MOV     [FILECNT],0                     ; No files transferred
        JMP     RET50

With COPY, the starter reports "copied EMPTY.ANS" and leaves no copy behind. XCOPY is an external program, copies empty files, and documents its codes: 0 normal, 2 Ctrl-Break, 4 "an error condition" (XCOPY.ASM lines 104-106). "Access denied" gives 4. A source that does not exist gives 0, the same as success, because the routine that prints "File not found" never touches the ERRORLEVEL byte:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.26 – XCOPY reports "File not found" without an error code (excerpt) (XCOPY.ASM lines 2831-2878)Source ↗
CHK_FILE_NOT_FOUND PROC NEAR
;if FILE_CNT_LOW=FILE_CNT_HIGH=FOUND_FILE_FLAG=0 AND NO INIT ERROR,
; then show "File not found" msg
;INPUT: ES, DS = data seg
⋮
            MOV     AX,MSG_FILE_NOT_ERR ;AN018;
            MOV     MSG_NUM,AX          ;AN000; set message number
            MOV     SUBST_COUNT,PARM_SUBST_ONE ;AN000; substitution count
            MOV     MSG_CLASS,UTILITY_MSG_CLASS ;AN000; message class
            MOV     INPUT_FLAG,NO_INPUT ;AN000; no input
            CALL    PRINT_STDOUT        ;AN000; display message
;       $ENDIF
$$IF169:

        RET

This is the gap that section 9.4 announced, of the same kind as FIND's. So BACKUP.BAT checks with IF NOT EXIST before it copies and trusts XCOPY's code only for the copy itself. PRINT_STDOUT also explains why "File not found" would disappear with >NUL while "Access denied" stays on the screen in Output 9.18: XCOPY writes its error messages with PRINT_STDERR (XCOPY.ASM lines 3690-3722), and COMMAND.COM cannot redirect standard error: its parser keeps one input and one output file name and no handle number (Module 3, section 3.4).

Patterns. FOR expands a word only if it contains a wildcard; then it calls Find First and Find Next and keeps the word's path prefix (A:\BACKUP.BAT). A word without a wildcard is copied as it is, and a wildcard with no match produces nothing at all:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.27 – How FOR expands a word of its list (excerpt) (TFOR.ASM lines 188-219)Source ↗
forsub:
        sub     CX, DX                          ; compute length of pathname prefix
        cmp     f.for_expand, 0                 ; are we still expanding a name?
        je      for_find_next                   ; if so, get next matching filename

        test    [BX].argflags, MASK wildcard
        jnz     for_find_first                  ; should we expand THIS (new) arg?
        mov     CX, [BX].arglen                 ; else, just copy all of it directly
        jmp     for_smoosh
⋮
for_result:
        mov     AX, -1                          ; assume worst case
        jc      forCheck
        mov     ax,0
forCheck:                                       ; Find* returns 0 for SUCCESS
        mov     f.FOR_EXPAND, AX                ; record success of findfirst/next
        or      AX, AX                          ; anything out there?
        jnz     for_begin                       ; if not, try next arg

for_smoosh:
        mov     SI, [BX].argpointer             ; copy argv[arg][0,CX] into destbuf
        mov     DI, OFFSET forbuf               ; some days this will be the entire
        rep     movsb                           ; arg, some days just the path prefix

So NOSUCH.DAT reaches the subroutine and fails, but *.XYZ disappears: BACKUP.BAT reports 0, 0 and 0 and exits with 0, and a mistyped pattern goes unnoticed. sh does the opposite. A pattern that matches nothing stays as it is (Lab 9.2), so backup.sh receives the literal *.dat and reports it as a failure. The kept prefix is also why the DOS script is limited to the current directory: for SUB\*.TXT it looks for the backup copy as SAVE\SUB\POEM.TXT, finds none, and copies the file into SAVE again on every run (we tried it: "copied" twice, never "same"). backup.sh takes the last component with ${f##*/}.

Redirecting a batch file. CALL A:\BACKUP.BAT ... >BAK.LOG created BAK.LOG and left it empty while the lines appeared on the screen. BatCom applies the redirection when it starts the batch file (TBATCH.ASM lines 688-692), but starting it is all that the "command" does. Back at TCOMMAND, HEADFIX (Listing 3.22) closes the file and restores the console before the first line of the batch file runs. COMMAND /C ... >BAK.LOG works, because the secondary shell inherits the file as its own standard output, and that is what its HEADFIX restores. sh treats a script like any other command: >bak.log 2>&1 catches all of it, cp's message included.

What "changed" means. BACKUP.BAT compares contents with FC /B, which reads both files completely. backup.sh compares modification times: test's -nt compares seconds and then nanoseconds (newerf, test.c lines 594-607), and cp -p copies the source's times to the copy with futimens (utils.c lines 343-349), so after a copy the two times are equal and the file counts as unchanged. Times are cheap to read but can lie: a file restored from an older copy is "not newer" even though it differs. A batch file has no way to compare two dates, and FAT stores times only to two seconds (Module 7), so the DOS script uses the more expensive but exact test.

Errors in sh. backup.sh checks every step with if and carries on. Run with sh -e, the same script stops at the first function that returns 1, here after nosuch.dat: no summary, y.ans not looked at, status 1. Commands tested by if, while, &&, || or ! are exempt from -e, so cp failing inside if cp -p ... never stops the script. -e is a safety net for scripts that check nothing; a script that checks everything gains nothing from it and may lose its summary. The DOS script has no such switch, and every check is an IF ERRORLEVEL or IF EXIST written by hand.

Questions.

  1. BACKUP.BAT saves %0 in BAKBAT before its first SHIFT. What would CALL %0 :ONE %%F run after one SHIFT? And if the user typed BACKUP without .BAT?
  2. Change BACKUP.BAT so that a pattern that matches nothing is reported as FAILED (hint: an environment variable cleared before the FOR and set by the subroutine).
  3. Give one case in which backup.sh skips a file that differs from its backup, and one in which it copies a file whose contents did not change. Change backup.sh to compare contents with cmp -s. What does each test cost for a 100 MB file?
  4. Why can BACKUP.BAT's summary not be printed as "6 copied, 0 unchanged, 1 failed", and what does the FIND /C trick cost compared with $((copied + 1))?
  5. Why does cp failing inside if not stop sh -e backup.sh, while backup_one returning 1 does? How would you keep -e and still get the summary?

Study cases#

Study case 9.A: 127 bytes or 512 KB: how long a command line can be#

Goal. Find out what each system does with a command line that is too long, and how the limit decided who expands the wildcards.

MS-DOS. The PSP has room for a command tail of 127 bytes (Table 9.1), and COMMAND.COM never builds a longer one: its command buffer, COMBUF, is COMBUFLEN = 128 bytes long, for typed lines and batch lines alike. A batch file is read one byte at a time, and every byte is counted, including the bytes substituted for %1 or %NAME% (TBATCH.ASM lines 416-424):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 9.28 – A batch line is cut at 128 bytes (excerpt) (TBATCH.ASM lines 288-357)Source ↗
RDBAT:
        invoke  GetBatByt
        inc     cx                              ; Inc the line length
        cmp     cx,COMBUFLEN                    ; Is it too long?
        jae     TooLong                         ; Yes - handle it, handle it
⋮
TooLong:
        ASSUME  DS:ResGroup
        cmp     al,0dh                          ; Has the end of the line been reached?
        jz      Ltlcont                         ; Yes, continue
        CALL    SkipToEOL                       ; Eat remainder of line

Ltlcont:
        stosb                                   ; Terminate the command
        jmp     Found_EOL                       ; Go process the valid part of the line

"Go process the valid part of the line": the rest is thrown away, and nothing is printed. We tried it with an argument of 150 digits in the AUTOEXEC.BAT that dos_run.py writes:

Output 9.21 – ARGS and ARGS.EXE with a 150-digit argument (captured with dos_run.py, CTTY COM1 first)
---- ARGS 1234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012
tail: 123 bytes [ 12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012]
0: [A:\ARGS.COM]
1: [12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012]
---- ARGS.EXE 123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678
argc: 2
0: [A:\ARGS.EXE]
1: [1234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678]

ARGS.COM received 122 of the 150 digits, and ARGS.EXE, whose name is four characters longer, 118. Each line of the generated AUTOEXEC.BAT ends with the >COM1 that dos_run.py adds, and that was cut off too, together with the end of the ECHO ---- ... line that prints the header. The output reached the capture only because CTTY COM1 had made COM1 the console. At a real keyboard the program would simply have run with a shorter argument and without the redirection.

With 127 bytes the shell cannot expand wildcards for the program: *.TXT in a directory of 200 files would need about 2,600. So on MS-DOS a program expands the pattern itself, with Find First and Find Next, after the tail has arrived. Every program that does so behaves a little differently:

  • COPY and XCOPY expand their own arguments and report "File not found" (Lab 9.7);
  • a C program expands only when it is linked with SETARGV.OBJ, sorts the names, and leaves a pattern that matches nothing as it is (Lab 9.2);
  • FOR expands inside COMMAND.COM and drops a pattern that matches nothing (Listing 9.27);
  • an assembly program expands nothing unless its author writes the loop (ARGS.COM, Lab 9.1).

FreeBSD. sh expands the patterns, and execve copies the arguments and the environment into a buffer of ARG_MAX bytes:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.29 – execve copies each string into the space left under ARG_MAX (excerpt) (kern_exec.c lines 1595-1616)Source ↗
        args->stringspace = ARG_MAX;
⋮
static int
exec_args_add_str(struct image_args *args, const char *str,
    enum uio_seg segflg, int *countp)
{
⋮
        error = (segflg == UIO_SYSSPACE) ?
            copystr(str, args->endp, args->stringspace, &length) :
            copyinstr(str, args->endp, args->stringspace, &length);
        if (error != 0)
                return (error == ENAMETOOLONG ? E2BIG : error);
        args->stringspace -= length;
        args->endp += length;

copyinstr fails with ENAMETOOLONG when a string does not fit into the space that is left, and execve returns E2BIG, "Argument list too long". The limit is four thousand times larger than on MS-DOS, but an expansion can still exceed it:

Output 9.22 – 100,000 arguments (captured in the course VM; the shell's message, on standard error, is printed last)
# jot 100000 | wc -c
  588895
# /bin/echo $(jot 100000) | wc -c
       0
sh: /bin/echo: Argument list too long
# jot 100000 | xargs /bin/echo | wc -lc
      20  588895

The numbers 1 to 100,000 take 588,895 bytes, more than the 524,288 of ARG_MAX. execve fails, sh reports it, and /bin/echo never runs: wc counts 0 bytes. xargs reads the words from its standard input instead and runs /bin/echo as often as needed, here 20 times: FreeBSD's xargs passes at most 5,000 arguments to one command, and never more bytes than ARG_MAX minus 4 KB minus the space the environment takes (xargs.c lines 131-143). find ... -exec cmd {} + does the same for file names.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Limit 127 bytes of tail; a 128-byte command buffer ARG_MAX = 512 KB for the arguments and the environment
Line too long the rest of a batch line is dropped without a message execve fails with E2BIG; the shell says so and nothing runs
Who expands *.TXT each program, in its own way the shell, the same way for every program
A pattern that matches nothing COPY, XCOPY: "File not found"; SETARGV: kept; FOR: dropped kept as it is; the program reports it
More names than fit the program loops over Find Next xargs, find -exec {} +

What to notice. The 127 bytes were fixed early: the command tail sits at offset 80h, where CP/M had put it. Once fixed, the limit forced wildcard expansion into the programs, and every program then expanded in its own way. FreeBSD pays for uniform expansion with a limit that only very long lists reach, and with a standard tool to get around it. Both systems can fail on a long line. MS-DOS runs a different command without saying so, and FreeBSD refuses to run anything and says why.

Discussion questions.

  1. A batch file builds a command from %1 to %9, each a long path. How could the batch file find out that the line was cut, given that COMMAND.COM prints nothing?
  2. echo $(jot 100000) | wc -c prints 588895 in the same shell. Why does the builtin echo work where /bin/echo failed?
  3. LINK accepts a response file, LINK @FILE (Module 5). Which problem of this study case does a response file solve, and which FreeBSD mechanism plays the same role?

Study case 9.B: What an exit code promises#

Goal. Compare what the standard utilities of each system promise with their exit codes, and so what a script can find out from them.

MS-DOS. The utilities that BACKUP.BAT relies on, asked the same three questions: "yes", "no", and "this cannot even be checked":

Output 9.23 – Exit codes of FIND, FC and XCOPY (captured with dos_run.py; EL.BAT prints ERRORLEVEL)
---- FIND "tool" POEM.TXT

---------- POEM.TXT
A small tool does one thing well:
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 0
---- FIND "mountain" POEM.TXT

---------- POEM.TXT
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 0
---- FIND "tool" NOSUCH.TXT
File not found - NOSUCH.TXT
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 0
---- FIND
FIND: Required parameter missing
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 2
---- FC Y.ANS Y.ANS
fc: no differences encountered
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 0
---- FC Y.ANS N.ANS
***** Y.ANS
y
***** N.ANS
n
*****

---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 1
---- FC Y.ANS NOSUCH.TXT
fc: cannot open NOSUCH.TXT - No such file or directory
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 1
---- XCOPY POEM.TXT
Reading source file(s)...
POEM.TXT
File cannot be copied onto itself
        0 File(s) copied
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 0
---- XCOPY
Invalid number of parameters
        0 File(s) copied
---- CALL A:\EL
exit code 4

FIND gives 0 for a match, for no match and for a missing file. Only a wrong command line gives 2 (section 9.4). FC is the most useful: 0 for "no differences" and 1 for everything else, so it cannot tell "different" from "cannot open". XCOPY has three documented values, but "File not found" (Lab 9.7) and "File cannot be copied onto itself" both give 0. COPY, being internal, sets nothing at all. None of this is a bug by the standards of 1988. Each utility's author chose its values, the only reader of an exit code was IF ERRORLEVEL in a batch file, and few batch files tested it.

FreeBSD. The same questions for grep, cmp and cp:

Output 9.24 – Exit codes of grep, cmp and cp (captured in the course VM)
# grep -q tool poem.txt; echo $?
0
# grep -q mountain poem.txt; echo $?
1
# grep -q tool nosuch 2>&1; echo $?
grep: nosuch: No such file or directory
2
# cmp -s poem.txt poem.txt; echo $?
0
# cmp -s poem.txt POEM.TXT; echo $?
1
# cmp -s poem.txt nosuch; echo $?
2
# cp 2>&1; echo $?
usage: cp [-R [-H | -L | -P]] [-f | -i | -n] [-alpsvx] source_file target_file
       cp [-R [-H | -L | -P]] [-f | -i | -n] [-alpsvx] source_file ... target_directory
64
# cp nosuch x 2>&1; echo $?
cp: nosuch: No such file or directory
1

grep and cmp follow the convention that POSIX writes into their specifications: 0 for "yes" (a match, the same contents), 1 for "no", and 2 or more for "I could not tell". A script can therefore separate an answer from a failure, as backup.sh does with cp. cp's 64 for a usage error comes from another convention, <sysexits.h>, which cp includes (utils.c lines 486-496: exit(EX_USAGE)) and which the header itself no longer recommends:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 9.30 – sysexits.h: codes from 64 up, deprecated for the base system (excerpt) (sysexits.h lines 36-97)Source ↗
 *  SYSEXITS.H -- Exit status codes for system programs.
 *
 *      This include file attempts to categorize error exit statuses
 *      for system programs, notably sendmail. These values exist only
 *      for interface compatibility, and are deprecated for FreeBSD
 *      base software.
⋮
#define EX_OK           0       /* successful termination */

#define EX__BASE        64      /* base value for error messages */

#define EX_USAGE        64      /* command line usage error */
Yes / success No / different Cannot check (missing file) Wrong usage
FIND 0 0 0 2
FC 0 1 1 1
XCOPY 0 – 0 ("File not found"); 4 for "Access denied" 4
COPY unchanged – unchanged unchanged
grep 0 1 2 2
cmp 0 1 2 2
cp 0 – 1 64

What to notice. An exit code is only as useful as the convention behind it. Both systems carry 8 bits from the program to the shell (section 9.4). The difference is that FreeBSD's tools agree on what the values mean and its shell tests them in every if, && and ||. A DOS batch file can trust FC and its own RC.COM and must check everything else another way, which is why BACKUP.BAT tests IF EXIST before it copies. The tools of this module follow the FreeBSD convention on both systems (section 9.6).

Discussion questions.

  1. Write the IF ERRORLEVEL lines that tell "different" from "cannot open" after FC A B. Is it possible? What would you test first?
  2. grep -q exits as soon as it finds a match. What happens to a long-running program whose output goes through a pipe into grep -q, and why can that change the exit status of prog | grep -q x under set -o pipefail?
  3. <sysexits.h> gives distinct values to 15 kinds of failure. Why would the FreeBSD developers deprecate it rather than adopt it everywhere?

Homework#

Hand in the source files, the build commands, transcripts of the runs and your answers as one archive. Build and run every MS-DOS program with tools/dos_tools.py (or NASM) and tools/dos_run.py --timeout, and every FreeBSD program in your VM. Cite source lines with permalinks as these notes do.

Exercise 9.1: HD with an offset and a length#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Add two options to HD (the C version, one source for both systems): -s offset skips that many bytes of the input, and -n length dumps at most that many bytes, as hexdump -s and -n do. The offsets printed must be offsets in the input, so HD -s 16 -n 32 COMMAND.COM starts with 00000010.

  1. Use fseek on a file and read-and-discard on standard input, which cannot seek on either system when it is a pipe. Test both paths on both systems.
  2. Accept offsets above 32,767: what type do you need in Microsoft C 5.10, and which function converts the argument?
  3. Compare your output on FreeBSD with hd -s 16 -n 32 on the same file, using cmp.
  4. What does -s mean together with -t on MS-DOS, where text mode removes bytes before you count them? Choose a behaviour, implement it and justify it in three sentences.

Deliverables: HD.C, transcripts from MS-DOS 4.00 and the VM, the answers to 2 and 4.

Exercise 9.2: Counting in parallel on FreeBSD#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

Write pwc, a C program for FreeBSD that counts the lines, words and bytes of one file with N processes: the parent forks N children, child i counts bytes [iS/N, (i+1)S/N) with pread(2), and sends its three counts and the first and last byte of its range back through a pipe(2). The parent adds the counts and corrects the words that a range boundary cut in two.

  1. Prove with a test that the correction is right: make a file in which a boundary falls inside a word, and compare with wc.
  2. Measure pwc with N = 1, 2 and 4 against wc on a file of at least 100 MB (concatenate /usr/share/dict/web2 many times) with time, twice in a row. Explain the difference between the first and the second run, and why more processes help little or not at all on the course VM.
  3. Why can this program not be written for MS-DOS 4.00 at all? Name the two missing mechanisms.

Deliverables: pwc.c, the test file generator, a table of times, the answers.

Exercise 9.3: A menu in a batch file#

Difficulty: introductory. Estimated time: 2 h.

Write MENU.BAT, which shows a menu (1 count the words of a file, 2 dump it, 3 show SYSINFO, Q quit), asks with ASK 123Q Choice, runs the chosen tool on the file named in %1 and comes back to the menu until the user types Q. Then write menu.sh with ask.sh on FreeBSD.

  1. Test MENU.BAT in two ways: with STUFF.COM (Lab 9.6), which puts the keys into the keyboard buffer, and with COMMAND /C MENU POEM.TXT <KEYS.TXT. Explain every difference, and what happens when KEYS.TXT ends before the Q (Lab 9.6). Always run with --timeout.
  2. What does each menu do when ASK returns 0 (no answer)? Make both stop cleanly.
  3. On MS-DOS the menu must use GOTO for the loop. Explain why FOR cannot loop until a condition becomes true.

End the last line of MENU.BAT with CR LF, like every other line; some editors leave it without one. When a batch file ends in a label such as :END with no line end, COMMAND.COM 4.00 meets the end of the file while it skips the label and returns without reading a new line (TBATCH.ASM lines 273-278), so the previous command runs a second time: a menu started without a file name prints its usage line twice. A GOTO END to that label ends the batch file inside GOTO (TBATCH2.ASM lines 669-689). If the batch file was started with CALL, its caller is never resumed, because only the path through ReadBat brings the caller back (TCODE.ASM lines 303-313), and COMMAND.COM waits for a command from the keyboard.

Deliverables: MENU.BAT, menu.sh, transcripts of a run with keys 1, 3, X and Q on each system.

Exercise 9.4: Port FreeBSD's cat to MS-DOS#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 6 h.

Port bin/cat/cat.c from the FreeBSD tree in this course to Microsoft C 5.10, with the options -b, -e, -n, -s, -t and -v (the cook_cat path) and without the rest. Keep the original structure where you can, and record every change in a table: line in cat.c, what you changed, why (missing header, missing function, 16-bit int, text mode, no Capsicum, no sockets), and the MS-DOS mechanism you used instead.

  1. Build CAT.EXE with tools/dos_tools.py and test it on CTRLZ.TXT and POEM.TXT, with and without -v. Should -v show the CR before each LF and the Ctrl-Z? Decide whether CAT opens files in text or binary mode, and defend the decision with a run. If the output on the screen stops at the Ctrl-Z, find the reason in the MS-DOS source before you work around it.
  2. cat.c has no getopt on MS-DOS. Write a small one or parse the options by hand, and say what you lost.
  3. Compare the size of CAT.EXE with that of FreeBSD's /bin/cat, and explain the difference.

Deliverables: CAT.C, the change table, transcripts.

Exercise 9.5: TEE on both systems#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write TEE, which copies standard input to standard output and to a file named as its argument, in assembly for MS-DOS (NASM, .COM) and in C for FreeBSD.

  1. Run WC POEM.TXT | TEE LOG.TXT on MS-DOS and ./wc poem.txt | ./tee log.txt on FreeBSD. Check that LOG.TXT and log.txt are byte-for-byte what the screen showed (use your HD).
  2. On FreeBSD, run (for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo $i; sleep 1; done) | ./tee log.txt. When does each line appear on the screen? When would it appear with a DOS pipe, and why (section 9.1, Module 3)?
  3. FreeBSD's tee also takes -a. Add it to both versions: which INT 21h function and which open(2) flag do you need?
  4. Run TEE NEW.TXT <CTRLZ.TXT and compare NEW.TXT with CTRLZ.TXT using FC /B. If TEE reports an error or the file is short, find the cause in the MS-DOS source and change TEE so that the file gets every byte.

Deliverables: TEE.ASM, tee.c, transcripts, the answers.

Exercise 9.6: Essay: writing a tool in 1988 and today#

Difficulty: introductory. Estimated time: 2 h.

Write 1,200 to 1,500 words comparing what it took to write a small command-line tool for MS-DOS 4.00 in 1988 and for FreeBSD 15.1 today: the interfaces the system offered, the tools that built the program, the conventions it could rely on, and how it could be tested. Support each claim with at least one source line (a permalink) or one measurement from your labs; use at least four of each. End with one thing that was easier in 1988.

Further reading#

  • Brian W. Kernighan and P. J. Plauger, Software Tools, Addison-Wesley, 1976: the book that defined the small tool reading standard input and writing standard output.
  • Brian W. Kernighan and Rob Pike, The UNIX Programming Environment, Prentice-Hall, 1984: chapters on the shell, filters and shell programming.
  • Ray Duncan, Advanced MS-DOS Programming, 2nd ed., Microsoft Press, 1988: the PSP, the command tail, the environment, handles, IOCTL and the exit code, from the program's side.
  • Ray Duncan (ed.), The MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Microsoft Press, 1988: batch files and the utilities' exit codes as documented at the time.
  • Ralf Brown's Interrupt List: INT 21h functions 01h, 08h, 30h, 36h, 3Fh, 40h, 44h, 48h, 4Ch and 4Dh.
  • IEEE Std 1003.1-2024 (POSIX.1-2024), Shell and Utilities volume: the "EXIT STATUS" sections of sh, grep, cmp, cp and xargs, and "Pattern Matching Notation".
  • Manual pages of the release: sh(1), test(1), cp(1), xargs(1), hexdump(1), wc(1), uname(3), sysctl(3), statfs(2), getcwd(3), elf_aux_info(3), sysexits(3), style(9).
  • The NASM manual, chapters on the bin and elf64 output formats.
  • Eric S. Raymond, The Art of Unix Programming, Addison-Wesley, 2003: chapter 1, on the rules of composition and silence that the tools of this module follow.
